Another promising area of research is graph-based reinforcement learning. Graph neural networks [336] in general have received much attention. Yet, in the surveyed literature, it has not been applied to a great extent in the energy domain as part of a reinforcement learning agent. However, graph structures appear naturally throughout the sustainable energy landscape. Prime examples would be (electrical) grids and chemical molecules. Those with interest in graph neural networks and reinforcement learning are strongly encouraged to apply their knowledge in the sustainable energy domain. Furthermore, multi-objective reinforcement learning [333] might also become relevant, since possible reward objectives, such as profit and emission reduction, can be conflicting. Multi-objective RL methods that can adaptively trade-off objectives thereby become relevant. In addition, also multiscale approaches hold promise. Especially the electricity grid has many subproblems that appear at different scales, and they all interact for overall grid efficiency. Some research does look at different scales of a problem simultaneously [215, 294], and integrating solutions is a promising avenue for future research. Finally, we point out that much research in the sustainable energy landscape relies on weather and energy price data. Future predictions of this data would be especially relevant for a wide variety of use cases. While some works attempt to include such prediction mechanics into their models, we believe the sustainable energy field would benefit most from addressing its own problems and using external models, developed in other fields, to address the challenges of timeseries prediction [337]. However, systems that accurately take history into account are a promising pathway for reinforcement learning in general. Due to the amount of timeseries data in the energy domain, this is especially relevant for sustainable energy research. As such, we believe that the recent advances in state-space-models [268, 269] may aid the performance of reinforcement learning agents in a wide variety of tasks discussed in this survey. Conclusion This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the available reinforcement learning approaches to sustainable energy challenges. We first of all observe that the research field has grown rapidly in recent years, and there are many sustainability challenges to which reinforcement learning is applicable. However, we also observe that most papers originate from energy researchers that start to apply reinforcement learning methodology, while reinforcement learning researchers are less present – probably because they struggle to understand the relevant underlying problems and the way

to model them. Therefore, to mature the field, we likely need more interaction between researchers from both communities. A key direction for integration would be the development of better benchmarks, that is, standardized test environments, on which we can test and compare reinforcement learning approaches. Even then, real-world deployment will probably also require the development of new core methodology, most notably in safe and offline RL. In short, this survey identifies a large potential for reinforcement learning to contribute to the sustainable energy transition. Given the urgency in solving these problems, we hope to see the field mature and interdisciplinary work thrive. An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning Bo Dai Georgia Institute of Technology bodai@cc.gatech.edu Yilun Du Harvard University ydu@seas.harvard.edu November 11, 2026 Abstract Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, pθ(x) ∝exp (−Eθ(x)), and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time. arXiv:2611.14383v1 [cs.AI] 10 Nov 2026

Discussion A Overview of Methods

Introduction Machine learning is often divided into supervised learning, generative modeling, representation learning, and decision making, each with its own models and training objectives. However, these areas share a common problem: learning relationships among variables and using those relationships to infer unknown quantities. Energy-based models (EBMs) provide a unified perspective on this problem by representing the compatibility of a configuration through a scalar energy function. Low-energy configurations correspond to plausible observations, compatible representations, or desirable outcomes. Learning shapes this energy landscape, while inference uses it to produce predictions, samples, or actions. This perspective connects three ideas: representation, inference, and composition. An energy function represents knowledge through relationships and constraints among variables. Inference uses this knowledge by searching for compatible configurations, either through optimization or sampling. Composition combines energy functions to express requirements that must be considered together. Separating these roles allows learned knowledge to be reused in different computations and combined with new information at inference time. For example, a joint energy over observations and latent variables can support both generating observations from a latent description and inferring a description from an observation. An energy over trajectories can be combined with a new goal to formulate a planning problem. In this tutorial, which grew from the course CSE 6243 taught by Bo Dai at Georgia Tech, we develop this perspective across different generative models, representation learning methods, and planning and reinforcement learning methods. We primarily consider the probabilistic formulation, in which an energy defines an unnormalized distribution through pθ(x) ∝exp(−Eθ(x)). For generative modeling, this provides a common language for comparing models that parameterize densities, learn scores, or construct sampling procedures. Autoregressive models specify conditional factors whose negative logarithms sum to an energy, while invertible normalizing flows specify densities through a change of variables. Diffusion models learn gradients of log densities at different noise levels. These connections clarify both the relationships among generative models and the different assumptions they make about representation and inference. They also provide a unified way to develop new generative models. For representation learning, energies express compatibility between observations and latent descriptions, or between different views of the same data. Contrastive methods learn features through scores for matched and mismatched observations, while reconstruction and denoising objectives train representations to support prediction of missing or corrupted information. Viewing these objectives through their associated energies connects representation learning to conditional prediction and generative modeling. It also suggests how learned generative models can provide objectives for inferring representations of new observations. For planning and decision-making, energies score candidate actions or trajectories according to their predicted consequences. Costs and constraints contribute energy terms, while rewards enter with the opposite sign. Planning searches for configurations that satisfy these requirements, and entropy-regularized formulations

Learned dynamics, behavior models, and task objectives can therefore contribute different components of a common inference problem. For inference-time computation, energies score different possible solutions for a question. Different methods of inference-time computation such as selecting among sampled responses, searching for partial solutions, or iteratively refining a candidate, correspond to different procedures to minimize this energy. Fine-tuning corresponds to directly fitting this combined energy, paying the cost of inference during training rather than for every input. Composition enables us to use these connections to solve new tasks. Energy functions over compatible variables can be added to combine their requirements, corresponding to a product of their unnormalized densities when the resulting distribution is normalizable. For example, an energy describing plausible robot trajectories can be combined with energies expressing a destination and obstacle constraints. The resulting inference problem uses learned knowledge together with task-specific information, without requiring a separate predictor to be trained for each combination. This ability to represent reusable components and reason with their combinations motivates the energy-based perspective. Its practical success depends on the accuracy and relative scales of the components, as well as the ability to optimize or sample from the composed landscape.

We begin with the formulation of EBMs and methods for inference and learning (Section 2). We then examine discriminative models (Section 3), generative models (Section 4), representation learning (Section 5), reinforcement learning and planning (Section 6), and inference-time compute (Section 7) through this common framework, and close with a discussion (Section 8). Throughout, we ask what each method represents, how inference uses that representation, and how its components can be combined or adapted to new tasks. Our aim is to explain connections among existing methods and show how those connections can guide the design of models that learn reusable knowledge and reason with it at inference time. A Brief Introduction to Energy-Based Models 2.1 Energy-Based Models We start with energy-based models of a single variable, which are also known as Gibbs distributions [75]. Formally, the EBM defines the density as pθ(x) = exp (−Eθ(x)) Zθ , with Zθ = Z exp (−Eθ(x)) dx, (1) where Eθ(x), known as the energy function, is some function parametrized with θ, and Zθ is known as the partition function, which is often unknown and intractable to compute. The EBM Equation 1 defines a valid distribution, satisfying the positivity pθ (x) ⩾0 and normalization R pθ (x) dx = 1. The value of the density pθ(x) in Equation 1 up to a multiplicative constant is fully determined by the energy function Eθ(x), enabling us to sample from the density even without knowledge of the normalization constants. EBMs can be easily generalized to joint or conditional models with multiple variables, respectively, i.e., pθ (x, y) = exp (−Eθ (x, y)) Zθ with Zθ = Z exp (−Eθ(x, y)) dxdy, (2) pθ (y | x) = exp (−Eθ (x, y)) Zθ(x) with Zθ(x) = Z exp (−Eθ(x, y)) dy. (3) By comparing the joint and conditional EBMs in Equation 2 and Equation 3, we emphasize the importance of partition function, leading to one key property of EBMs: with the same energy function but different partition functions, we can represent and sample from the corresponding conditional or joint distributions. Although this property seems trivial, it will play a vital role in enabling compositionality, adaptivity, and improving training data sample complexity. In comparison to many classes of generative models, EBMs Equation 1 directly model the probability density, without any forms of factorization of the distribution to enable efficient sampling. As a result, for many distributions, it can be simpler to represent the distributions as EBMs than other factorized parameterizations, at the cost of much more expensive inference. As noted after Equation 3, a joint energy also defines the conditional distribution obtained by fixing any subset of its variables, and only the partition function changes. Energies can further be added, subtracted, and combined, which forms new distributions from learned ones without retraining [49, 50]. Let c1, . . . , cn be conditions on x, such as attributes of an image or requirements on a trajectory, and suppose we have an unconditional EBM p(x) ∝exp (−E(x)) and a conditional EBM p(x | ci) ∝exp (−E(x | ci)) for each condition alone. If the conditions are conditionally independent given x, then p(x | c1, . . . , cn) ∝p(x) n Y i=1 p(ci | x) ∝p(x) n Y i=1 p(x | ci) p(x) , E(x | c1, . . . , cn) = E(x) + n X i=1 (E(x | ci) −E(x)) , (23) up to constants that do not depend on x [117].

Each difference E(x | ci) −E(x) equals −log p(ci | x) up to a constant, i.e., it is the energy of an implicit classifier, so the conjunction adds one classifier energy per condition to a single prior, which is counted once rather than n times. Weighting the differences gives the guided distributions of Section 4.3, with n = 1 for classifier-free guidance, and adding the difference for c1 while subtracting the one for c2 gives the negation p(x) p(c1 | x)/p(c2 | x), an inversion Equation 22 whose negated expert is the implicit classifier of c2. The derivation makes two requirements explicit. First, the

conditions must be conditionally independent given x, which holds, for example, when each condition is a function of x. Second, each p(x | ci) must be accurate where the composition places its mass, a region that may contain few training examples for any single condition. The first is a modeling assumption, and the second determines how far a composition generalizes beyond its training data. What Does Composition Do? Composition reuses learned components in new combinations. Each component describes one aspect of the data or the task, such as a concept, a constraint, a dynamics model, or a goal, and may be a separately trained model or a conditional model evaluated under one condition. Components may also be defined over different subsets of the variables, in which case the composed energy is an MRF Equation 9 whose factors are learned separately and whose graph is chosen for each task, as when the constraints among objects in a scene are composed into a factor graph over their poses [197]. Since the components are learned separately, training needs to cover each component but not each combination. Suppose x is described by K conditions, each taking one of M values. A single model of p(x | c1, . . . , cK) must be trained on enough of the M K combinations, whereas the composition Equation 23 only requires the KM conditionals p(x | ck), and it generates combinations that never appear together in the training data [53, 117]. The same operations recur throughout this tutorial: guided sampling multiplies a diffusion model by a classifier (Section 4.3), planners compose dynamics, goals, and obstacles (Section 6.5), and reasoning composes the energies of individual constraints into larger problems (Section 7.3). The product Equation 20 has the form of a product of experts [87], which uses it to model a single distribution with jointly trained experts; composition uses it to combine models trained separately. See Du and Kaelbling [50] for a broader discussion. Adaptation. The same operations adapt a pretrained model to new data or requirements without retraining it. Conditioning is the simplest case: by Equation 2 and Equation 3, clamping any subset of the variables of a joint energy, such as the visible pixels of an image or the start and goal of a trajectory, turns the same energy into a conditional model, and MCMC never needs the new partition function. A residual energy adapts a model to new data: by Equation 4, p(x) ∝p0(x) exp  −˜Eθ(x)  keeps a pretrained p0 fixed and learns only ˜Eθ, which can be small when the new distribution is close to the old one. This is the structure of the KL-regularized fine-tuning of language models in Section 6.1,

Finally, a new requirement is a new energy term: the planning problems of Section 6.5 adapt a model of trajectories to a goal and constraints by adding their energies. Sampling from Compositions. A composed energy is sampled or minimized with the methods of Section 2.4, which need the composed energy or its gradient but not the partition function. Three practical issues remain. First, reading a sum of energies as a product of distributions requires each energy to be a log-density up to a constant. Energies trained by regression (Section 2.5) or with a margin (Section 3) are not maximum likelihood fits, and for them the sum is better read as an objective, as in the set operations above: its minimizers satisfy all requirements when the requirements are compatible, and prediction by energy minimization Equation 35 applies directly. Second, separately trained energies have no common scale, so the weights in P i wiEi act as inverse temperatures that must be chosen at inference time. Third, the modes of a product lie where all components agree, which can be a small region far from the modes of each component, so the composed landscape is harder to sample than its parts. Annealing through smoothed energies helps, and diffusion models provide such a sequence for each component; however, adding their scores at a noise level does not give the score of the smoothed product, so Langevin or MCMC corrections on the summed energies are needed to sample the composition correctly (Section 4.3) [55].

2.4 Inference with EBMs In this section, we first introduce the approximate algorithms for calculating the corresponding probability distributions induced by EBMs, which can be largely categorized in two classes: Metropolis–Hastings algorithm via generating samples and variational inference via distribution approximation. Then, we introduce prediction by optimization, which returns a single output rather than samples. We mainly discuss the inference methods for unconditional EBMs Equation 2, however, the algorithms can be easily generalized for conditional EBMs Equation 3. Metropolis-Hastings Sampling. Since Zθ is intractable, we cannot sample from or calculate the probability of pθ(x) ∝exp (−Eθ(x)) directly. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) instead constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is pθ, and treats the states of the chain after a burn-in period as approximate samples. The Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithm [125, 85] is the general recipe: given the current state x, it draws a candidate x′ ∼q(x′ | x) from a proposal distribution and accepts it with probability α (x, x′) = min  1, exp (−Eθ(x′)) q(x | x′) exp (−Eθ(x)) q(x′ | x)  , (24) otherwise staying at x. The partition function cancels in the ratio, so only energy differences Eθ(x′)−Eθ(x) are required, and the acceptance step guarantees detailed balance with respect to pθ for any valid proposal. Different MH samplers differ only in the choice of q, which determines how the energy function is used. The Gibbs sampler [72] updates one variable (or block of variables) at a time, using the full conditional pθ(xi | x−i) as the proposal. With this choice of q, the acceptance probability in Equation 24 is always one, which means the candidate is always accepted. The conditionals only involve the energy terms that contain xi, which makes Gibbs sampling natural for MRFs and Boltzmann machines. Particularly, in RBMs, the conditional independence of y given x and vice versa allows each layer to be sampled in one block. For continuous x and differentiable energies, the gradient ∇xEθ(x) provides a much better proposal than random perturbations. Langevin dynamics follows the gradient with injected noise, x(t+1) = x(t) −η∇xEθ  x(t) + p 2η ξ(t), ξ(t) ∼N (0, I) , (25) which converges to pθ as η →0. With a finite step size, the update is biased; using Equation 25 as the proposal of an MH step removes the bias, yielding the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA) [147]. In practice, many EBM learning methods run the unadjusted version for a fixed number of steps. Langevin dynamics moves by a small random step at each iteration, so it explores the space slowly, like a random walk. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) [59, 131] avoids this by borrowing the dynamics of a physical particle. It introduces an auxiliary

In practice, many EBM learning methods run the unadjusted version for a fixed number of steps. Langevin dynamics moves by a small random step at each iteration, so it explores the space slowly, like a random walk. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) [59, 131] avoids this by borrowing the dynamics of a physical particle. It introduces an auxiliary momentum v ∈Rd and defines the Hamiltonian H(x, v) = Eθ(x) + 1 2∥v∥2 2, (26) i.e., a potential energy Eθ(x) plus a kinetic energy. The joint distribution p(x, v) ∝exp (−H(x, v)) = pθ(x) N (v; 0, I) has pθ as its marginal on x, so it suffices to sample from the joint and discard v. Each HMC iteration first resamples the momentum v ∼N (0, I), and then moves (x, v) along Hamilton’s equations, dx dt = v, dv dt = −∇xEθ(x). (27) The particle speeds up when rolling down the energy landscape and slows down when climbing, while the total energy H stays constant. Hence it can travel far from its starting point to a state of similar probability. Since Equation 27 cannot be solved exactly, it is simulated for L steps of the leapfrog integrator with step size ϵ, v ←v −ϵ 2∇xEθ(x), x ←x + ϵv, v ←v −ϵ 2∇xEθ(x). (28)

The leapfrog integrator is reversible and preserves volume, so the end point (x′, v′) can be used as an MH proposal with a simple acceptance probability min {1, exp (H(x, v) −H(x′, v′))}, which corrects the discretization error. Because the leapfrog integrator nearly conserves H, this probability stays close to one even for distant proposals. HMC thus trades more gradient evaluations per sample (L per iteration) for much less correlated samples. Its performance depends on ϵ and L: a large ϵ lowers the acceptance rate, while a poorly chosen L wastes computation or makes the trajectory turn back on itself. The No-U-Turn sampler [91] balances this trade-off by setting L adaptively. With a single leapfrog step (L = 1), HMC reduces to MALA with step size η = ϵ2/2. The exact samplers above, general MH, Gibbs sampling, MALA, and HMC, are all special cases of the MH algorithm; unadjusted Langevin dynamics is not, and does not sample exactly from pθ at a finite step size. These samplers place different requirements on the energy function: general MH and Gibbs sampling only need to evaluate energies (or conditionals), and therefore apply to discrete and structured spaces, whereas Langevin dynamics and HMC need the gradient ∇xEθ, and therefore require continuous inputs and differentiable energies. Amortized Sampling via Variational Inference. MCMC samplers pay their cost for every sample: each new sample requires running a chain for many steps, and consecutive samples are correlated. Variational inference takes a different route: it fits a tractable distribution qϕ(x) to approximate EBM pθ, so that afterwards drawing a sample costs only one pass through qϕ; the cost of inference is thus amortized over all samples. The standard objective is minimizing the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence, min qϕ KL (qϕ∥pθ) = Ex∼qϕ [Eθ(x)] −H (qϕ) + log Zθ, (29) where H (qϕ) = −Eqϕ [log qϕ(x)] is the entropy of qϕ. Since log Zθ does not depend on ϕ, we can fit qϕ by minimizing Eqϕ [Eθ(x)]−H (qϕ), which never evaluates the intractable partition function. The first term pulls the samples toward low-energy regions, and the entropy term keeps them spread out instead of collapsing onto a single minimum. Because the KL divergence is non-negative, Equation 29 also yields the variational lower bound log Zθ ⩾Ex∼qϕ [−Eθ(x)] + H (qϕ) , (30) which is tight if and only if qϕ = pθ. Therefore, the same optimization provides both a sampler and an estimate of the log-partition function, which can also be used for learning EBMs. The only remaining part is that the parametrization choice of qϕ needs to make both sampling and the entropy tractable. The difficulty is that ϕ appears in the distribution the expectation is taken over. There are two standard estimators. For continuous x and an implicit or reparameterizable qϕ, i.e., x = gϕ(z) with z ∼N (0, I), the reparameterization trick [103] moves ϕ inside the expectation, ∇ϕEz [Eθ (gϕ(z))] = Ez "∂gϕ(z) ∂ϕ ⊤ ∇xEθ (gϕ(z)) # , (31) which again uses ∇xEθ. The derivative of log qϕ inside the expectation drops out because Eqϕ [∇ϕ log qϕ(x)] = 0; for the same reason, any constant

baseline b can be subtracted without introducing bias. REINFORCE only needs to evaluate the energy and the log-density of qϕ at the samples, so it applies to any x, including discrete and structured outputs. Its price is high variance, as it only uses the value of the energy rather than its gradient. Therefore, in practice, a baseline b, e.g., the average of Eθ(x)+log qϕ(x) over the other samples in a batch, or other control variates are necessary to make it work. In short, the two estimators trade generality for variance: the reparameterization estimator Equation 31 uses the gradient of the energy and usually has much lower variance, but requires continuous x, a differentiable Eθ, and a reparameterizable qϕ; REINFORCE Equation 32 only needs energy values and log qϕ, and so applies to discrete or non-differentiable settings, at the cost of higher variance. When both are applicable, the reparameterization estimator is generally preferred. Compared with MCMC, variational inference is fast at sampling time but biased: the error is limited by the family of qϕ, and the reverse KL Equation 29 is mode-seeking, so qϕ tends to miss some modes of pθ. The two can be combined [36]: a learned qϕ can provide initializations for short MCMC chains, or serve as the proposal in an MH step, whose acceptance probability Equation 24 then corrects the bias of qϕ. The obstacle is again the partition function: Zθ depends on θ, so the likelihood and its gradient cannot be computed directly. Learning methods for EBMs differ mainly in how they avoid or approximate Zθ, as we will discuss in the following.

Maximum Likelihood Estimation. Given a dataset D = {X}, the most direct approach to learning an energy function Eθ(x) is through maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). We can directly fit a probability density pθ(x) ∝exp(−Eθ(x)) to maximize the log-likelihood of samples drawn from a dataset D, i.e., minimizing the negative log-likelihood. The full form of the likelihood of Eθ(x) as defined in Equation 1 is exp(−Eθ(x))/Z, where Z is the partition function. The negative log-likelihood loss objective is given by LNLL(D) = Ex∼D[−log(pθ(x))], (37) which can be equivalently written as LNLL(D) = Ex∼D[Eθ(x)] + log Z exp(−Eθ(x))dx  . (38) Taking the gradient of the above objective, we obtain the expression ∇θLNLL(D) = Ex∼D[∇θEθ(x)] − R exp(−Eθ(x))∇θEθ(x)dx R exp(−Eθ(x))dx , (39) where we can reduce the right-hand side to the expectation ∇θLNLL(D) = Ex∼D[∇θEθ(x)] −Ex∼pθ(x)[∇θEθ(x)]. (40) Using the above expression, the gradient of LNLL can be computed equivalently from the surrogate loss eLNLL(D) = Ex∼D[Eθ(x)] −Ex∼stopgrad(pθ(x))[Eθ(x)], (41) which gives us a simple objective for training Eθ(x) through maximum likelihood estimation, where we contrastively decrease the energy of ground truth data samples while increasing the energy of samples drawn from the model distribution x ∼pθ(x). However, in practice, drawing samples from the distribution pθ(x) can be challenging – several approaches to drawing these samples were discussed in Section 2.4. Particularly, in the original contrastive divergence, these negative samples are initialized from ground truth data [87], while one can also initialize samples from random noise or an approximate distribution and use Langevin dynamics to draw negative samples to train the EBM [51, 36]. In general, pseudolikelihood is a consistent estimator of the overall distribution p(x), as long as the distribution is positive at every data point x [21, 95]. However, in comparison to other approaches for training EBMs, pseudolikelihood focuses on local interactions between variables. This can make the method data inefficient when fitting distributions where there are global interactions between multiple variables. Connection to masked discrete diffusion. Pseudolikelihood is closely related to masked, or absorbingstate, discrete diffusion models [9, 150, 157]. Both are trained to predict hidden variables from visible ones. Pseudolikelihood hides exactly one variable xj and fits pθ(xj | x−j). Masked diffusion hides a random subset M of the variables, whose size ranges from one variable to all of them, and fits pθ(xj | x−M) for every j ∈M. With the linear noise schedule, its training objective is a weighted average of such masked-prediction losses over masking ratios, LMD(θ) = Et∼U[0,1]  1 t EM∼qt  − X j∈M log pθ (xj | x−M)    , (51) where qt hides each variable independently with probability t. Pseudolikelihood Equation 50 is the special case in which exactly one variable is hidden at a time. The link is even closer in continuous time: the score of a discrete diffusion model can be written through the single-variable conditionals pt(xj | x−j), exactly the quantities pseudolikelihood fits, and it can be learned by a categorical ratio matching objective built on them [165]. Pseudolikelihood keeps only the last term of each ordering, k = d, where every other variable is visible. It is therefore not a bound on the likelihood, and it never trains the model to predict a variable whose neighbors are also unknown, which is why it struggles with the global interactions mentioned above. In an EBM, every conditional is derived from a single energy function, so the conditionals are always consistent with one joint distribution. Masked diffusion models usually parameterize the conditionals directly with a neural network, and the learned conditionals need not agree with any joint distribution. The two also sample differently: Gibbs sampling resamples one variable at a time from the pseudolikelihood conditionals and keeps cycling, whereas masked diffusion starts with every variable hidden and reveals them progressively until none are left. For continuous x, this gradient is the score, ∇x log pθ(x) = −∇xEθ(x) −∇x log Zθ = −∇xEθ(x), (52) and Zθ drops out because it does not depend on x. Score matching fits the model score to the data score by minimizing their expected squared distance, the Fisher divergence, LESM(θ) = 1 2 Ex∼pd h ∇x log pθ(x) −∇x log pd(x) i . (53)

The data score ∇x log pd is unknown, but Hyv¨arinen [94] showed by integration by parts that, under mild smoothness and boundary conditions, Equation 53 equals, up to a constant that does not depend on θ, LSM(θ) = Ex∼pd 1 ∇xEθ(x) 2 −tr �∇2 xEθ(x)  , (54) which only involves the energy and the data. The trace of the Hessian in Equation 54 needs d backward passes, which is expensive in high dimensions. Sliced score matching [162] projects the scores onto random directions v and replaces the trace with v⊤∇2 xEθ(x) v, which needs a single Hessian-vector product. Denoising score matching [182] removes the second derivative altogether. It adds Gaussian noise to the data, ˜x = x + σϵ with ϵ ∼N (0, I), and matches the model score at ˜x to the score of the noising kernel, which is known in closed form, LDSM(θ) = 1 2 Ex∼pd, ϵ  −∇˜xEθ(˜x) + ˜x −x σ2  . (55) Its minimizer is the score of the noisy data distribution rather than of pd itself, which approaches the data score as σ →0. Limitations. Because the score is a local quantity, score matching sees each region of the space only through how the density changes there. Where the data are scarce, as in the low-density regions between separated modes, the learned score is inaccurate, and Langevin sampling from it mixes poorly between modes [161]; the noise in denoising score matching helps by filling in these regions. Score matching also requires continuous x and a differentiable energy. For discrete data, ratio matching [96] plays the same role by matching ratios pθ(x′)/pθ(x) between states that differ in a single variable, in which Zθ again cancels. These ratios are determined by the single-variable conditionals pθ(xj | x−j), which ties score matching for discrete data back to pseudolikelihood and to the categorical ratio matching used in discrete diffusion [165]. Adversarial training starts from maximum likelihood and removes the partition function with the variational bound from Section 2.4. The negative log-likelihood Equation 38 contains log Zθ, and by Equation 30, log Zθ is itself the solution of an optimization problem over distributions, log Zθ = max q Ex∼q [−Eθ(x)] + H (q) , (56) where the maximum is attained at q = pθ. Substituting Equation 56 into Equation 38 turns maximum likelihood into a min-max problem, min θ LNLL(θ) = min θ max q Ex∼pd [Eθ(x)] −Ex∼q [Eθ(x)] + H (q) . (57) The two players have clear roles. For a fixed energy, the inner maximization over q is exactly the variational inference problem Equation 29: it fits q to pθ by minimizing KL (q∥pθ), so q becomes an amortized sampler for the current EBM. For a fixed q, the gradient of the outer objective with respect to θ is Ex∼pd [∇θEθ(x)] −Ex∼q [∇θEθ(x)] , (58) which is the maximum likelihood gradient Equation 40 with the samples from pθ replaced by samples from q. The energy thus lowers itself on data and raises itself on the sampler’s outputs, while the sampler moves its samples toward low energy and keeps them spread out through the entropy term. No MCMC is run during training; the sampler is learned instead. This is the structure of a generative adversarial network [77]: the energy plays the discriminator and q plays the generator. The difference is the entropy term H (q). Without it, the inner maximization would put

all of q’s mass at the minimum of the energy, which is the mode collapse familiar from GANs, and the game would no longer correspond to maximum likelihood. With it, the solution of Equation 57 is the maximum likelihood estimate, and the learned generator is a sampler for the learned EBM [101, 39]. The entropy is also what makes the method hard in practice. It is easy to compute only for restricted families of q, such as normalizing flows [146]. For flexible implicit generators x = gϕ(z), it has to be estimated or bounded, and different estimates lead to different algorithms [101, 39]. One alternative defines q by a few steps of learnable sampling dynamics, such as Langevin or Hamiltonian updates started from a simple distribution, whose entropy can be tracked through the dynamics [36]; the dual view of Equation 57 also extends to kernel exponential families [35]. A second difficulty is that for a fixed q the objective in Equation 57 is only a lower bound on the negative log-likelihood, since q only lower-bounds log Zθ. If q falls behind the current energy, minimizing over θ lowers the bound rather than the likelihood. In practice, θ and q are updated in alternation, and the quality of the learned EBM depends on how closely q tracks pθ. Regression Training. Energy functions can also be learned through regression objectives that supervise the outputs or updates of energy minimization. The supervision need not specify scalar energy values: it can instead describe where optimization should arrive or how a candidate should move [38]. IREM and Equilibrium Matching illustrate these two approaches. Regressing optimized predictions. Iterative Reasoning through Energy Minimization (IREM) [54] learns a conditional energy Eθ(x, y) by supervising the prediction obtained after minimizing it. Given a paired input and solution (x, y), initialize ˆy(0) and perform K updates, ˆy(k+1) = ˆy(k) −η∇yEθ(x, ˆy(k)). (59) The regression objective is LIREM(θ) = E(x,y)∼D, ˆy(0) h ∥ˆy(K) −y∥2 i . In practice, IREM truncates backpropagation to the final update and uses a replay buffer of optimized candidates alongside random initializations. Generative Models Many existing generative models can be viewed as special cases of EBMs. Each defines, explicitly or implicitly, a distribution pθ(x) ∝exp (−Eθ(x)), and they differ mainly in how they handle two parts that Section 2 treated separately: the potential function Eθ and the sampler that draws from it. A general EBM parameterizes the potential freely, so it can express any shape, but it must pay at sampling time, with MCMC or a learned sampler, and at training time, with the methods of Section 2.5. Other generative models restrict or learn one of the two parts so that the other becomes easy. The following subsections take the main families in turn. In GANs, the generator plays the role of the learned sampler in adversarial training and the discriminator plays the role of the potential; adding an entropy term on the generator turns the pair into an EBM trained by maximum likelihood. Normalizing flows build the sampler as an invertible map, which makes the potential, including its normalization, exact by change of variables. Diffusion and flow-matching models learn the gradient of the potential at many noise levels and sample by following it, as in annealed Langevin dynamics. Energy-inspired models take a sampler that uses a learned potential as the model itself, so that sampling is exact and the likelihood has a tractable bound; modern Hopfield networks, discussed alongside them, retrieve stored patterns by energy minimization; and deep equilibrium models define a layer by the fixed point of an iterative update, such as energy minimization. Finally, autoregressive models write the potential as a sum of normalized conditionals, which makes sampling one variable at a time exact.

4.1 Generative Adversarial Nets The adversarial training of Section 2.5 already has the structure of a GAN. We make the correspondence explicit, and then use it to read the original GAN and its variants from the EBM view. Entropy-Regularized GAN. Take the sampler q in Equation 57 to be an implicit generator, x = gϕ(z) with z ∼N (0, I), and write qϕ for its distribution. Maximum likelihood for the EBM becomes min θ max ϕ Ex∼pd [Eθ(x)] −Ez [Eθ (gϕ(z))] + H (qϕ) . (76) The energy acts as the discriminator: it is lowered on data and raised on generated samples. The generator moves its samples toward low energy, while the entropy term keeps them spread out. The two players have the same roles as in Section 2.5, and so does the result. If both families are rich enough, the solution satisfies qϕ = pθ = pd: the energy recovers −log pd up to a constant, and the generator is a sampler for it. Training yields both parts of the EBM, the potential and the sampler [101, 39, 36]. The practical difficulty is the one noted in Section 2.5: the entropy of an implicit generator has no closed form and must be estimated or bounded. The Original GAN. The original GAN [77] trains a discriminator D(x) = sigm (ℓ(x)) to tell data from generated samples, min ϕ max ℓ Ex∼pd [log sigm (ℓ(x))] + Ez [log (1 −sigm (ℓ(gϕ(z))))] . The discriminator objective in Equation 77 is binary NCE Equation 44 with ν = 1 and the generator as the noise distribution. Second, the generator update has no entropy term, so the generator’s best response is not tied to an EBM. For a fixed energy, the entropy-regularized generator maximizes −Eq [Eθ] + H (q) = −KL (q∥pθ) + log Zθ, whose unique maximizer is the EBM itself, q = pθ ∝exp (−Eθ). Without the entropy, the generator only maximizes −Eq [Eθ], or, in Equation 77, minimizes Eq [log (1 −sigm(ℓ))]; in both cases, the best response is a point mass at the minimum of the energy, or at the maximum of ℓ. The EBM is then just one of the distributions the generator may settle on, with no force pulling it there, and the game can reach solutions outside the space of EBMs, such as a generator that covers only some modes of the data; this is one source of mode collapse. The entropy term in Equation 76 addresses both points: it makes the generator’s objective KL (qϕ∥pθ), so every solution of the game is an EBM, and it keeps the discriminator a valid energy at the solution. Both require the generator’s density: the entropy H (qϕ) = −Eqϕ [log qϕ] requires log qϕ, which is exactly what an implicit generator lacks. This is why entropy-regularized GANs either use generators with tractable densities or estimate the entropy, as discussed in Section 2.5. Other GAN Variants. Several GAN variants change the discriminator loss, and the EBM view classifies them by how the loss shapes the potential. Each loss relaxes the constraints that an EBM places on the model: the potential need not be normalized, and the generator need not sample from it. The f-GAN [134] replaces the Jensen–Shannon divergence with any f-divergence through its variational representation. The energy has two terms: how unlikely the corresponding latent point is under the base distribution, and how much the flow compresses or expands volume at x. This special parametrization makes the partition function of the EBM tractable: it equals one for every θ, because the change of variables preserves total mass. More generally, if the base distribution is itself an EBM, p0 ∝exp (−E0) with partition function Z0, then the same argument shows that the flow has partition function Z0 as well. A flow never changes the partition function; it moves the normalization into the base distribution, where it is known. Learning and Sampling. Because Zθ does not depend on θ, maximum likelihood is exact. In the gradient Equation 40, the expectation under the model equals −∇θ log Zθ = 0, so the negative phase vanishes and the gradient reduces to Ex∼pd [∇θEθ(x)], with no samples from the model needed during training. Sampling is also exact and takes one pass: draw z ∼p0 and return gθ(z). A flow therefore makes both parts of the EBM easy at once, the potential with its normalization and the sampler. Normalizing Flows and General EBMs. Since a flow has an exact density, and hence an exact entropy, it is a natural choice for the learned sampler in adversarial training Equation 57 and in variational inference [146], which is the first difficulty noted for implicit generators in Section 4.1. A flow can also serve as the noise distribution of NCE Equation 44, where its exact density is what NCE needs; flow contrastive estimation trains the flow and the EBM jointly, so that the noise stays close to the data [70]. Limitations. The tractability comes from architectural constraints. The map must be invertible, so x and z have the same dimension and there is no bottleneck, and each layer must have a cheap Jacobian determinant, which limits how much each layer can do. Invertibility also preserves topology: mapping a unimodal Gaussian onto data with separated modes requires very steep transformations between the modes. A general EBM has none of these constraints, but pays with an intractable partition function. This is the trade-off described at the start of this section: flows restrict the potential so that its normalization and its sampler come for free. 4.3 Diffusion and Flow Models Diffusion and flow models generate data by gradually transforming noise into samples. We first introduce both families in their usual form, and then use Tweedie’s formula to show that they learn a sequence of EBMs, one for each noise level, and differ from EBMs mainly in how they parameterize it. Diffusion Models. A diffusion model [160, 90, 163] fixes a forward process that corrupts a data point x0 ∼pd with Gaussian noise of increasing scale. All we need is its marginal at each time, xt = αtx0 + σtϵ, ϵ ∼N (0, I) , t ∈[0, 1], (80) that is, xt | x0 ∼N �αtx0, σ2 t I  . The schedule satisfies α0 = 1 and σ0 = 0, and the signal-to-noise ratio α2 t/σ2 t decreases to nearly zero at t = 1. Variance-preserving diffusion takes α2 t + σ2 t = 1, variance-exploding diffusion takes αt = 1 with σt growing large, and the linear interpolation αt = 1 −t, σt = t is used by rectified flow. Let pt denote the distribution of xt. To generate data, the process is run backward in time, from noise at t = 1 to data at t = 0, by the reverse-time stochastic differential equation or the deterministic probability-flow ordinary differential equation [163]. Both only require the score ∇x log pt(x) at every t. Diffusion models learn it with a network ϵθ(xt, t) trained to predict the noise that was added, L(θ) = Et, x0∼pd, ϵ h w(t) ϵθ (αtx0 + σtϵ, t) −ϵ i , (81) with a weighting w(t) over noise levels. At each t, this is denoising score matching Equation 55 [182], which corresponds to αt = 1, generalized to αt̸ = 1, as made precise below.

Flow Models. Flow matching and rectified flow [115, 119, 3] use the same interpolation Equation 80 between data and noise, but learn the velocity of the path instead of the noise. The network vθ(xt, t) is regressed onto the time derivative of the interpolation, L(θ) = Et, x0∼pd, ϵ h vθ (xt, t) −( ˙αtx0 + ˙σtϵ) i , (82) and samples are generated by integrating the ordinary differential equation dxt/dt = vθ(xt, t) from noise to data. Some works use the reverse time convention, with noise at t = 0; we follow the diffusion convention throughout. The minimizer of Equation 82 is the conditional expectation v⋆(x, t) = ˙αtE [x0 | xt = x] + ˙σtE [ϵ | xt = x]. Tweedie’s Formula. The two families, and their different targets, are connected by Tweedie’s formula [61]. Since pt(x) = R pd(x0) N �x; αtx0, σ2 t I  dx0, differentiating under the integral gives ∇xpt(x) = R pd(x0) N �x; αtx0, σ2 t I  αtx0−x σ2 t dx0, and dividing by pt(x) yields ∇x log pt(x) = αt E [x0 | xt = x] −x σ2 t , equivalently E [x0 | xt = x] = x + σ2 t ∇x log pt(x) αt . Energy-inspired models (EIMs) [107], proposed before this view of diffusion models became common, share the same spirit from a different direction: they focus on the sampling procedure of the EBM during learning. A general EBM is sampled with an approximate procedure, such as MCMC or importance sampling, so the samples we actually use come from the sampler, not from the model pθ, and training the energy as if the samples were exact creates a mismatch between the model and the inference procedure. EIMs remove the mismatch by taking the distribution induced by the sampler, which uses a learned energy, as the model itself, and maximizing its likelihood directly. In terms of the two parts of Section 4, an EIM keeps the energy but defines the distribution through the sampler, so that sampling is exact by construction. Self-Normalized Importance Sampling. to the deep equilibrium models of Section 4.5. 4.5 Deep Equilibrium Models Inference in an EBM is often energy minimization, carried out by iterating a fixed update until it stops changing. Deep equilibrium models (DEQs) [10] take this iteration as the definition of a network layer: the output is the point where the update no longer changes it. Used as a generator, a DEQ can be viewed as an energy-inspired model (Section 4.4) whose sampler is a deterministic fixed-point solver: draw noise z ∼p0, iterate the update to its fixed point, and return it. When the update is a gradient step on an energy, this sampler is energy minimization started from the noise. Fixed-Point Layers. Given an input x and a layer fθ, a DEQ defines its output as the fixed point z⋆= fθ (z⋆, x) . (92) This corresponds to applying the same layer infinitely many times, a weight-tied network of infinite depth, but the fixed point is found directly by a root-finding method, such as Broyden’s method or Anderson acceleration, applied to gθ(z) = fθ(z, x)−z. Training does not backpropagate through the solver’s iterations. By the implicit function theorem, the gradient of a loss ℓ(z⋆) is ∂ℓ ∂θ = ∂ℓ ∂z⋆  I −∂fθ(z⋆, x) ∂z⋆ −1 ∂fθ(z⋆, x) ∂θ , (93) which depends only on the fixed point, so memory does not grow with the number of solver steps. The vector–inverse-Jacobian product is itself computed by solving a linear fixed-point equation.

Learning DEQs. How a DEQ is trained depends on whether a target is available for its fixed point. In the conditional setting, each input x comes with a target output y, and learning is easy: a task loss is placed on the fixed point and differentiated through it, L(θ) = E(x,y)∼D [ℓ(hθ (z⋆ θ(x)) , y)] , z⋆ θ(x) = fθ (z⋆ θ(x), x) , (94) where hθ is an output head and ℓis, for example, the cross-entropy for classification or the squared error for regression. The exact gradient is the implicit gradient Equation 93 [10]; cheaper approximations drop or truncate the inverse-Jacobian term, such as Jacobian-free backpropagation [192] and phantom gradients [73], and penalizing the Jacobian of the update keeps the fixed point stable during training [11]. Energy minimization trained by regression onto the solution, as in IREM [54], falls in this setting as well. The unconditional setting, where the goal is to learn a distribution and no output is paired with the noise, is harder, and existing methods first turn it into a problem that has a target or a likelihood: distillation from a pretrained diffusion model, which supplies noise–sample pairs and reduces generation to regression [74]; an invertible fixed-point map, which gives an exact likelihood as in normalizing flows [121]; a fixed-point layer inside the denoiser of a diffusion model, trained from scratch with the denoising loss of Section 4.3 [12]; and Equilibrium Matching, which learns a time-independent gradient field whose descent from noise reaches the data [186]. Equilibrium Matching is the closest to a DEQ trained without a teacher, since its sampler is exactly the fixed-point iteration of Equation 92 with the energy-descent layer fθ(z) = z −η∇zEθ(z). As introduced in Section 2.5, it corrupts data as xγ = (1 −γ)x + γϵ with γ ∼U[0, 1] and ϵ ∼N (0, I), and regresses the gradient of the energy at xγ onto (ϵ −x) c(γ), Equation 62. Two choices turn this regression into a fixed-point model. First, the network does not receive γ, so the minimizer is the single field ∇E⋆(z) = E [(ϵ −x) c(γ) | xγ = z], averaged over all noise levels that could have produced z, rather than a family indexed by time as in diffusion. Second, the magnitude satisfies c(0) = 0, for example c(γ) = γ, so the target vanishes at the data, and data points are equilibria of the field. This holds only approximately: since the field averages over noise levels, a data point is an exact equilibrium only if the corrupted samples that land on it come almost entirely from γ ≈0. Connection to EBMs. Choose the layer to be one step of gradient descent on an energy, fθ(z, x) = z −η∇zEθ(x, z). Its fixed points are exactly the stationary points of the energy, ∇zEθ(x, z⋆) = 0, so the forward pass of the DEQ is energy minimization, as in Section 2.4, and Equation 93 differentiates through the minimizer without unrolling it. This is the exact counterpart of the unrolled training of end-to-end SPENs in Section 3.2 and of IREM in Section 2.5, which backpropagate through a fixed number of minimization steps. The converse does not hold: a general layer fθ is not the gradient of any scalar function, because the Jacobian of a gradient field is symmetric while that of a general layer is not. A general DEQ therefore computes an equilibrium that is not the minimum of any energy, and its fixed point may not exist or be unique. Monotone operator equilibrium networks [191] restrict the layer so that a unique fixed point is guaranteed, and the modern Hopfield networks of Section 4.4 are an instance in which the update does descend an explicit energy. 4.6 Autoregressive Models as Approximate Ancestral Samplers Autoregressive models can be viewed as another reparameterization of an EBM from the sampler’s point of view, in the spirit of the energy-inspired models of Section 4.4. Instead of parameterizing a global energy

and then designing a sampler for it, the parameterization follows ancestral sampling: each step models the conditional distribution of one variable given the ones already generated, and the joint distribution is the one induced by a single sweep in a fixed order. Fixed-Order Factorization of an EBM. For x = (x1, . . . , xd) with each xi in a finite vocabulary V, any EBM Equation 1 factorizes exactly in a fixed order by the chain rule, pθ(x) = d Y i=1 pθ(xi | x<i), pθ(xi | x<i) = P x>i exp (−Eθ(x)) P xi, x>i exp (−Eθ(x)). (96) Drawing x1, then x2 given x1, and so on, is ancestral sampling: each variable is drawn given the ones already visited, with the unvisited ones marginalized out, and this single pass returns an exact sample. Unlike a Gibbs sweep (Section 2.4), which conditions on the current values of all other variables and revisits them, it draws each variable once. For a general EBM, however, the sum over x>i is as intractable as Zθ itself. Autoregressive models reparameterize exactly this sum: they model it directly with a network eθ, X x>i exp (−Eθ(x)) ≈exp (−eθ(xi; x<i)) , (97) which turns the exact conditional in Equation 96 into pθ(xi = v | x<i) = exp (−eθ(v; x<i)) P v′∈V exp (−eθ(v′; x<i)). (98) The marginalization over the unvisited variables is never computed; it is absorbed into eθ, which plays the role of the free energy of x⩽i after x>i is summed out. What remains is a normalization over the |V| values of a single variable, with −eθ(·; x<i) as the logits, i.e., the multi-class logistic regression of Section 3. An autoregressive model is therefore ancestral sampling of Equation 96 with its intractable conditionals replaced by learned ones. NADE [178] gives a concrete instance: its forward pass is a single pass of mean-field inference that approximates the conditionals p(xi | x<i) of an RBM, with the unvisited variables initialized to zero rather than summed out, and its weight sharing is inherited from the RBM. Exact Learning. The same factorization makes learning exact: maximum likelihood decomposes into a sum of per-step cross-entropies, L(θ) = −Ex∼pd " d X i=1 log pθ(xi | x<i) # , (99) each of which is the exact maximum likelihood of a conditional EBM Equation 98, and all of which can be computed in parallel from a data sequence. Both fit single-variable conditionals that are softmaxes over V, and both are tractable for the same reason: only the normalization of one variable over |V| values is needed. They

Pseudolikelihood Equation 50 is the closest learning method for EBMs, and comparing the two shows what the reparameterization changes. Both fit single-variable conditionals that are softmaxes over V, and both are tractable for the same reason: only the normalization of one variable over |V| values is needed. They differ in the conditioning set (Figure 5). Pseudolikelihood fits the full conditionals pθ(xj | x−j), the steps of the Gibbs sampler of Section 2.4, which can be computed from Eθ in closed form because nothing is summed out. An autoregressive model fits the chain-rule conditionals pθ(xi | x<i), the steps of ancestral sampling in Equation 96, which require summing out x>i and are therefore reparameterized by eθ. This single difference leads to opposite trade-offs: • Objective. By the chain rule, Equation 99 is exactly the negative log-likelihood, so autoregressive training is exact MLE. The sum of full conditionals in Equation 50 is not a likelihood. In the ordering view of Section 2.5, pseudolikelihood keeps only the last term of every ordering, whereas an autoregressive model keeps all the terms of one fixed ordering.

Averaging Equation 99 over random orders gives an any-order autoregressive model [177, 92], and, as discussed with pseudolikelihood in Section 2.5, the masked discrete diffusion objective Equation 51 is equivalent to it [136]. On the gain side, sampling takes a single exact pass of Equation 98 with no burn-in or mixing, and learning is exact maximum likelihood Equation 99, since each step only requires a normalization over |V| values. On the cost side, eθ is no longer tied to a global energy. In Equation 96, all conditionals are derived from a single Eθ, whereas an autoregressive model approximates each marginalized sum separately, so in general the parameters of an underlying EBM cannot be recovered from it. Moreover, summing out x>i couples variables that Eθ does not couple directly: even when Eθ is simple, such as a pairwise MRF with few parameters, the sums P x>i exp (−Eθ(x)) are generally complex functions of the whole prefix x<i, and they change with the chosen order. Approximating them by exp (−eθ) therefore requires a far more flexible eθ than the energy it replaces, and the compact structure of Eθ is lost.

Large Language Models (LLMs). LLMs are the setting in which this reparameterization fits best, since both of its costs are naturally mitigated. First, the order is given. Text is a sequence, and the left-to-right order in which it is written and read is a natural choice for the fixed order in Equation 96, so no ordering has to be chosen or learned [20]. Second, the marginalized sums in Equation 97 are modeled by a highly flexible network. A Transformer decoder [180] computes −eθ(·; x<i) as the logits over the token vocabulary from the entire prefix, which provides exactly the flexibility over the whole context that the approximation requires. With causal masking, all d conditionals in Equation 99 are computed in one forward pass over a training sequence, so learning remains exact maximum likelihood at scale [139, 24], and generation is ancestral sampling, one token at a time. Representation Learning So far, the energy itself has been the object of interest: in Section 3 it scores outputs for prediction, and in Section 4 it defines the distribution to sample from. In representation learning, the energy becomes a means rather than an end. The goal is a feature map ϕθ(x) that is useful for downstream tasks, and the energy is the pretext through which it is learned: ϕθ is placed inside an energy defined on a self-supervised task, such as matching two views of the same input, predicting the masked parts of an input, or denoising a corrupted input, and the energy is trained with one of the methods of Section 2.5. After training, the energy is discarded and ϕθ is kept. From this view, self-supervised methods differ mainly in two choices, the structure of the energy and the learning method, and the learning methods they use are precisely those that avoid sampling from the model. 5.1 Contrastive Representation Learning Following Dai et al. Connection to Masked Discrete Diffusion and Pseudolikelihood. Starting from BERT, its masking ratio t0 connects it to the two objectives related in Section 2.5. [9] make the second connection precise: BERT is a one-step discrete diffusion model, whose transition matrix mixes the absorbing state [MASK] with a uniform transition, matching BERT’s practice of replacing some selected tokens by [MASK] and others by random tokens. Denoising avoids both. We first derive the classical denoising autoencoder [183, 182] from a joint EBM over the input and a latent variable; the derived model justifies the bilinear structure of Equation 100, with the DAE as a conditional EBM of this form. Diffusion Spectral Representation. The diffusion spectral representation keeps the conditional bilinear form Equation 100 and extends the DAE in three ways. The condition is a separate clean variable x, such as an image, a prompt, or a state–action pair, rather than a corrupted copy of the target; the target is a corrupted variable ˜y, at every noise level t of the forward process Equation 80, ˜y = αty + σtϵ, with one representation ϕθ(x) shared across noise levels; and the target features µθ(˜y, t) are nonlinear, so the partition function over ˜y is no longer available, and the model is learned by score matching instead of maximum likelihood. The DAE and the diffusion spectral representation are thus the same kind of conditional EBM, with the DAE as the single-level special case whose condition is the corrupted input itself, in the same way that BERT is the single-level special case of masked diffusion in Section 5.3. For discrete targets such as text, the Gaussian corruption is replaced by masking and the regression by the masked diffusion loss [37, Sec. 7.2], which returns to the bilinear denoising EBM of BERT Equation 112. 5.5 Representation-Induced Decisive Models Many uses of large language models are decisions rather than open-ended generation: classifying an input, judging whether a response satisfies a requirement, or retrieving the documents that answer a request. A generative LLM makes such a decision by decoding text, which takes a full autoregressive pass and returns a string rather than a distribution over the possible answers. Such inference is expensive: each decision costs one forward pass per generated token, often including a long reasoning trace, and estimating the distribution over the answers requires sampling many responses. Decisive foundation models [176] instead turn each query into a discriminative question: they take a context, a query, and a set of candidate answers, and return a distribution over the candidates. Unlike the discriminative models of Section 3, whose classes are fixed in advance, the classes of a decisive model are specified by the instruction and vary from one query to another. Instruction-following retrievers [205] implement decisive foundation models by generalizing embedding models. Instruction-Following Retrieval. Instruction-following retrieval asks for the contexts X, such as passages of a corpus, that satisfy an instructional query Q = (I, q), which consists of a query q and an instruction I that specifies requirements such as a perspective, format, or level of detail, and possibly the candidate answers. Each pair (X, Q) thus poses a discriminative question with a yes-or-no answer: does X satisfy Q?

InF-Embed [205] generalizes an embedding model to answer it. The score is the cosine similarity between the embeddings of the two sides, sθ(X, Q) = x⊤q ∥x∥2 ∥q∥2 , x = gX θ (X), q = gQ θ (I, q), (127) where gX θ is the context encoder, and the instructional-query encoder gQ θ either encodes the concatenation of the instruction and the query, or encodes them separately and combines their embeddings by crossattention. The score serves as the logit of the answer: with the two candidates yes and no, pθ(yes | X, Q) = σ (sθ(X, Q) + b) with an offset b, and when the instruction lists K candidate answers, each candidate receives a score and the answer distribution is the softmax of the scores over the K candidates, of which the logistic form is the case K = 2. Retrieval asks this question for every context in the corpus and ranks the contexts by their scores; since the context encoder does not depend on the query, the context embeddings can be precomputed and indexed offline, so answering a new query costs only one encoding of the query and one inner product per context, which makes inference fast and scalable to large corpora with approximate nearest-neighbor search. Generalizing Embedding Models. Standard embedding models such as BERT [44] learn an embedding x of the data only, and each new downstream question requires training a new classifier w⊤x on top of it. In InF-Embed, the context embedding plays the same role, but the more important part is the embedding head gQ θ for the query and the instruction, which maps each instructional query to the weights q = gQ θ (I, q) of this classifier. A new question is therefore answered at inference time by one encoding, without training a new classifier, and the same context can be relevant to one instruction and irrelevant to another. InF-Embed thus generalizes embedding models from embedding the data to also embedding the questions asked about it, while the context embeddings remain query-independent and can still be precomputed. InF-Embed learns the score by ranking NCE Equation 47: treating the score as a potential on both sides, it fits the conditionals of the contexts given the query and of the queries given the context. As in CLIP (Section 5.1), fitting both conditionals trains both sides of the energy, and replacing one side at a time keeps the denominator linear in the batch size. The training data supply the noise distribution: each positive pair (X, Q) with Q = (I, q) comes with two negative pairs (X− 1 , (I−, q)) and (X− 2 , (I, q−)), in which an LLM alters the instruction or the query slightly so that a different context becomes relevant. These hard negatives bring the noise distribution close to the data, which makes NCE statistically efficient, and they force the energy to depend on the instruction rather than on the query alone. From Embeddings to Decisions. InF-Embed is a bilinear representation following Equation 100, with the context and the instructional query on the two sides. The major difference is in how it is used: in representation learning, the energy is discarded after training and the embedding is used alone for downstream tasks, whereas a decisive foundation model uses the learned model itself, which generalizes across queries and instructions, to make the decision. In general, the instructional query Q itself may contain the candidate answers, which form a set O(Q), and the decision is pθ(o | X, Q) = exp �ϕθ(X)⊤ψo θ(Q)  P o′∈O(Q) exp �ϕθ(X)⊤ψo′ θ (Q) , o ∈O(Q), (129)

where ϕθ encodes the context, and ψθ encodes the instructional query once and returns an embedding ψo θ(Q) for each of its candidates. InF-Embed is the case of the two candidates yes and no, whose logit ϕθ(X)⊤(ψyes θ (Q) −ψno θ (Q)) is parameterized by the score Equation 127. The main difference from an LLM, which is also a softmax over bilinear energies, is that the potential in Equation 129 encodes the entire instructional query Q at once and gives the answer in a single step, whereas an LLM factorizes the answer autoregressively and generates it token by token, each step a softmax over the vocabulary. Hence a decision costs one forward pass rather than one per generated token, which makes inference much faster than with an LLM. Reinforcement Learning and Planning through EBMs EBMs enter reinforcement learning (RL) at several levels, depending on which part of the decision-making problem the energy models. In model-free RL, the energy is placed on the actions only: adding an entropy or KL regularizer to the reward or to the policy update makes the optimal policy an EBM over actions at each state, whose energy is the negative Q-function (Section 6.1). Acting with such a policy requires sampling from this EBM (Section 6.2), and inverse RL and imitation learning fit EBMs over actions or trajectories to expert demonstrations (Section 6.3). Beyond the policy, the energy can be placed on the dynamics themselves, where an EBM world model yields a representation in which value functions are linear and can be learned by temporal-difference learning (Section 6.4), and on whole trajectories, where planning becomes inference in a trajectory EBM that composes dynamics, behavior priors, goals, and constraints (Section 6.5). 6.1 Naturally Induced EBM Policies Entropy-Regularized MDP. Consider a Markov decision process with states s, actions a, reward r(s, a), transition P(s′ | s, a), and discount γ ∈(0, 1). Maximum-entropy RL seeks the policy π⋆= argmax π Eπ " ∞ X t=0 γt (r(st, at) + λ H (π(· | st))) # , (130) where H is the entropy and λ > 0 is a temperature. Its solution is an EBM over actions, whose energy is the negative soft Q-function and whose log-partition function is the soft value function, π⋆(a | s) = exp Q⋆(s, a) −V ⋆(s) λ  , V ⋆(s) = λ log X a exp Q⋆(s, a) λ  , Q⋆(s, a) = r(s, a) + γ Es′∼P (·|s,a) [V ⋆(s′)] . (131) The last two equations form the soft Bellman equation, which replaces the max over actions in the standard Bellman optimality equation by a log-sum-exp, and recovers it as λ →0. The entropy-regularized objective Equation 130 has been proposed from

(131) The last two equations form the soft Bellman equation, which replaces the max over actions in the standard Bellman optimality equation by a log-sum-exp, and recovers it as λ →0. The entropy-regularized objective Equation 130 has been proposed from several different motivations, all of which lead to the same EBM Equation 131: • Probabilistic inference. Maximum-entropy inverse RL [206] applies the maximum entropy principle (Section 2) to trajectories, and control as inference [109] casts optimal control as posterior inference in a graphical model whose potentials are exponentiated rewards. • Tractability. Linearly-solvable MDPs [171] penalize the KL divergence of the controlled dynamics from passive dynamics, which makes the Bellman equation linear in the exponentiated value, so that optimal control reduces to an eigenvalue problem. • Optimization smoothing. SBEED [34] interprets the entropy as Nesterov smoothing of the nonsmooth max in the Bellman optimality equation, using that the negative entropy is the convex conjugate of log-sum-exp. The smoothed Bellman operator remains a contraction, and the smoothed Bellman equation admits a primal–dual reformulation that yields a convergent algorithm with nonlinear function approximation. The same operator appears as an alternative softmax operator for value updates [7].

• Robustness to noise. Viewing the policy as a channel with limited information, Rubin et al. [148] trade value against information, and soft Q-learning [66] uses the resulting soft updates to reduce the overestimation bias caused by noisy value estimates. Maximum-entropy RL also provably solves certain robust RL problems with perturbed rewards and dynamics [62]. Conversely, robustness to uncertain dynamics induces the same exponential form on the transition side: in soft robust MDPs, an adversary perturbs the transition kernel subject to a KL penalty, the worst case is the tilted kernel ˜P(s′ | s, a) ∝P(s′ | s, a) exp (−V (s′)/λ), an EBM over next states, and the problem is equivalent to a risk-sensitive MDP with the entropic risk measure [201]. • Exploration. The entropy keeps the policy stochastic, and path consistency learning [128], soft Qlearning [83], and soft actor–critic [84] use it to explore multiple modes of the action space. • Unifying valueand policy-based methods. With the entropy, soft Q-learning and policy gradient methods become equivalent [153], and both are instances of a single convex-optimization view of entropy-regularized MDPs [132]. Whatever the motivation, the outcome is an EBM: acting is sampling from Equation 131, and learning amounts to fitting its energy, so the tools of Section 2 apply directly. KL-Regularized Policy Updates. The entropy in Equation 130 modifies the MDP itself. A different use of the KL divergence keeps the vanilla MDP, i.e., λ = 0, and regularizes each policy update instead. Given the current policy πk, trust-region and mirror-descent policy optimization [152, 154, 71] improve the policy while penalizing, or constraining, its KL divergence from πk. In the penalized form, πk+1(· | s) = argmax π Ea∼π [Qπk(s, a)]−1 η KL (π ∥πk(· | s)) =⇒ πk+1(a | s) ∝πk(a | s) exp (η Qπk(s, a)) . Unrolling the recursion from π0 gives πk(a | s) ∝π0(a | s) exp  η P j<k Qπj(s, a)  , an EBM whose energy accumulates the Q-functions of all previous iterates. Unlike Equation 131, the temperature is not fixed: the energy grows with k, so the iterates concentrate on the greedy actions and converge to the optimal policy of the vanilla MDP. The KL thus regularizes the optimization path rather than the solution, and the EBM structure appears in every update rather than at the optimum. KL regularization can also be taken toward a fixed reference policy π0 rather than the previous iterate, which changes the objective rather than the update; the optimal policy is then the residual EBM with base measure π0. The optimization is thus easy, but acting requires sampling actions from these EBMs, which brings back the sampling difficulty of Section 2.4. For discrete actions, the partition function is a sum over |A| actions, the policy is a softmax over Q-values, and sampling is exact. For continuous actions, the partition function is an integral, and the commonly used methods fall into the following three classes.

Variational Policy Optimization. The first restricts the policy to a family πϕ that is easy to sample from, such as a Gaussian with the reparameterization trick, and optimizes Equation 130 or Equation 132 within this family. By the variational bound Equation 30, this projects the EBM onto the family, max ϕ Ea∼πϕ(·|s) [Q(s, a)] + λ H (πϕ(· | s)) = −λ KL  πϕ(· | s) exp (Q(s, ·)/λ) Z(s)  + λ log Z(s), max ϕ Ea∼πϕ(·|s) [Qπk(s, a)] −1 η KL (πϕ(· | s) ∥πk(· | s)) . Sampling is cheap, but the family limits the policy: a Gaussian cannot represent the multimodal EBMs that arise when several actions are nearly optimal. MCMC Sampling. The second samples from the EBM directly. The score of the policy is the action gradient of the Q-function, ∇a log π(a | s) = ∇aQ(s, a)/λ, so Langevin dynamics Equation 25 draws actions by a ←a + ϵ λ∇aQ(s, a) + √ 2ϵ ξ. Planning versus Policies. Policies and planners represent the same EBM at different levels. For deterministic dynamics, the trajectory EBM Equation 153 factorizes along the trajectory into the soft-optimal policy given by Equation 131, as shown for maximum-entropy IRL in Section 6.3. A policy amortizes planning into one network for one reward and acts in a single forward pass. A planner keeps the terms of Equation 154 separate and pays with sampling or optimization at every decision, but a new goal, cost, or

constraint only requires a new energy term rather than a new policy. This is the trade-off between amortized sampling and MCMC in Section 2.4, and between learning the policy and learning the reward in Section 6.3, now applied to acting. Inference-Time Computation A recent source of improvement in large models is to spend more computation per input at inference time rather than at training time. In the EBM view, these procedures are samplers or optimizers for one distribution, the composition of a pretrained generator with a verifier, which is the KL-regularized EBM of Section 6.1. We first describe this target, then view common inference-time methods as the samplers of Section 2.4, Section 4.4, and Section 6.5, then show how composing learned energies supports reasoning on problems larger than those seen in training, and finally relate inference-time computation to fine-tuning, which amortizes the same sampler. 7.1 Verifiers Define the Target Let π0(y | x) be a pretrained generator, such as a language model that answers a prompt x with a response y = (y1, . . . , yT ), and let r(x, y) be a verifier that scores complete responses, such as a learned reward model, a learned verifier [32], or a checker such as unit tests. The target of inference-time computation is the residual EBM π⋆(y | x) = π0(y | x) exp (r(x, y)/λ) Z(x) , Z(x) = Ey∼π0(·|x) [exp (r(x, y)/λ)] , (156) which is the optimal policy of the KL-regularized objective Equation 137, with the prompt as the state and the response as the action. The temperature λ trades the verifier against the generator. For a binary verifier, r ∈{0, 1}, the limit λ →0 gives π⋆(y | x) = π0(y | x, r = 1), the generator conditioned on being correct, which is the product of π0 with the set energy Equation 15 of correct responses, the logical AND of Section 2.3. Several verifiers compose in the same way, as π0 Q k exp (rk/λk), e.g., for a correctness check and a style or safety reward. The verifier can even be the generator’s own likelihood, which sharpens the generator without any external signal, as discussed in Section 7.2. Since verifiers are learned or incomplete, the temperature also limits how far the target moves from the generator, as measured by KL (π⋆∥π0), and thus how much an inaccurate verifier can be exploited. This is the requirement of Section 2.3 that each component be accurate where the composition places its mass. The target is a distribution, and the prediction can be a sample from it or its mode. The simplest methods draw N complete responses y1, . . . , yN ∼ π0(· | x) and use the verifier only to select among them. Returning yi with probability proportional to exp (r(x, yi)/λ) is the self-normalized importance sampler of Section 4.4 with the generator as the proposal: it samples a distribution that interpolates between π0 and π⋆, and converges to π⋆as N →∞. Best-of-N, which returns the response with the highest reward, is also a residual EBM. Many reasoning problems, however, are defined by constraints on parts of their solutions. Each clause of a 3-SAT problem involves three variables, a valid coloring of a graph gives different colors to the two endpoints of every edge, and a solution of the N-queens problem places one queen in every row and column and at most one on every diagonal.
