Each clause of a 3-SAT problem involves three variables, a valid coloring of a graph gives different colors to the two endpoints of every edge, and a solution of the N-queens problem places one queen in every row and column and at most one on every diagonal. A network trained end to end to map problems to solutions must learn this whole map from examples, and it often fails on problems larger than those it was trained on. The energy view suggests a different decomposition, illustrated in Figure 14: learn an energy for each kind of constraint, compose the energies of the constraints that appear in a new problem, and solve the problem by minimizing the composition [135].

Composed Energies. We write a problem x as a set of constraints c1, . . . , cK, where ck involves the variables ySk of the solution, such as the two endpoints of an edge or the three variables of a clause. An energy Eθ(c, yS) that is low on the assignments satisfying a single constraint is composed into the energy of the whole problem, E(x, y) = K X k=1 Eθ (ck, ySk) , (162) which is an MRF Equation 9 whose factors share one learned energy and whose graph is given by the problem. When a solution exists, the minimizers of Equation 162 satisfy every constraint, which is the logical AND Equation 16 of Section 2.3. A problem with more variables and constraints than any training problem is a longer sum of the same terms, so training needs to cover the kinds of constraints rather than their combinations, which is the sample-complexity argument of Section 2.3 applied to reasoning. Oarga and Du [135] train such energies on single clauses of 3-SAT, single edges of graph coloring, and the rows of one N-queens solution, using the energy-parameterized denoising objective of Section 4.3 together with a contrastive loss that raises the energy of invalid assignments (Section 2.5). They compose the energies over whole problems, including SAT instances and graphs larger than any used in training, and, since a sum of separately trained energies can have spurious minima, they can fine-tune the composition on complete solutions. Minimizing the Composition. The composed energy is harder to minimize than any of its terms: its minima are where all terms agree, it is non-convex, and gradient descent or Langevin dynamics Equation 25 from a single initialization is easily trapped. Oarga and Du [135] minimize it with parallel energy minimization (PEM), an SMC procedure over the noise levels of the energy: a population of candidates starts from noise, and at each level, the candidates are resampled in proportion to exp (−E), perturbed with noise, and moved by a gradient step on the energy at that level. Resampling discards candidates in poor local minima, and the noise keeps the population spread over different solutions. More candidates solve more problems, so the computation spent at inference can grow with the difficulty of a problem, which a network that predicts the solution in a single pass cannot do. With this sampler, the composed energies outperform learned solvers trained end to end on most of the N-queens, 3-SAT, and graph-coloring benchmarks considered, including their larger instances [135]. This distribution reweights the pretrained model π0 toward responses with higher verifier scores. Fine-tuning amortizes this computation into the generator’s weights: it learns a model πθ that approximates the target across inputs, allowing high-reward responses to be generated with less search at inference time. Below, we discuss three approaches to learning such a model.

RL Fine-Tuning. KL-regularized RL rewards high verifier scores while keeping the model close to π0. Substituting the definition of π⋆into its objective gives Ey∼πθ(·|x) [r(x, y)] −λ KL (πθ ∥π0) = −λ KL (πθ ∥π⋆) + λ log Z(x). (163) Since Z(x) does not depend on θ, maximizing this objective is equivalent to minimizing the reverse KL to the target, as in variational inference (Equation 29) and policy learning (Equation 133). This objective is often mode-seeking: when πθ cannot match π⋆exactly, it may concentrate on a few high-probability regions of the target. Practical algorithms build on this objective. GRPO [156], for example, uses REINFORCE-style policy gradients (Equation 32) with rewards normalized within a group of responses to the same prompt. It subtracts the group’s mean reward and divides by its standard deviation, then combines these normalized rewards with PPO-style clipping and a KL penalty to the reference model. Rejection-Sampling Fine-Tuning. A second approach uses the verifier to construct a training dataset. For each input, we sample several responses from π0, discard those that fail the verifier, and train the model on those that pass. This is the basic idea behind methods such as STaR [199] and RFT [198], and it amortizes the rejection sampler of Section 7.2 into the weights of πθ. For a binary verifier, r ∈{0, 1}, the accepted responses are exact samples of π⋆(y | x) = π0(y | x, r = 1), the λ →0 limit of the target (Section 7.1), which keeps the relative probabilities that π0 assigns to correct responses and removes the incorrect ones. The expected log-likelihood of these responses is Ey∼π⋆(·|x) [log πθ(y | x)] = −KL (π⋆∥πθ) −H (π⋆) . (164) Since H (π⋆) does not depend on θ, maximum-likelihood training minimizes the forward KL to π⋆. For a binary verifier, the target of RL fine-tuning in Equation 163 tends to the same π⋆as λ →0, but optimizes the KL in the opposite direction. If a fixed number of responses is sampled per prompt and the accepted ones are pooled, each prompt is weighted by its pass rate under π0, so prompts that π0 does not solve are not trained on. The forward KL is mass-covering and when πθ cannot match π⋆exactly, it spreads its probability over all the successful solutions found during sampling, and may also place probability on responses that fail. A proposal concentrated on only a few solutions may rarely generate other responses favored by the target. Tradeoff Between Finetuning and Inference. More broadly, fine-tuning pays a training cost to reduce search across many later inputs, sometimes making a single sample sufficient. Inference-time methods spend computation on each input but can adapt to a new verifier without retraining the generator. The same trade-off appears between learned samplers and MCMC in Section 2.4, and between policies and planners in Section 6.5: computation can be spent during training to make later inference cheaper, or during inference to adapt to the problem at hand. 7.5 Best-of-N Sampling-Aware Fine-Tuning One round of best-of-N distillation (Section 7.4) makes πθ only as good as best-of-N of π0. To improve further, iterative BOND distills best-of-N of the distilled model again, round after round, and by Yang et al. [196] these rounds reach the WIND equilibrium Equation 166 only after distilling repeatedly until convergence. This motivates a different approach: keep best-of-N with a fixed N at inference time, and update the base policy for it directly. Inference-aware fine-tuning [31] places the loss not on πθ but on the distribution πBoN of the response that best-of-N returns from πθ, as compared in Figure 15. Since only the

best of N samples is used, πθ does not need to put most of its mass on good responses; it only needs one of its N samples to be good, which leaves room for diverse responses. Best-of-N Policy as an EBM. Best-of-N selects by an arg max over N samples, which cannot be differentiated with respect to θ. Its output distribution, however, has an explicit density: by Equation 157 with πθ in place of π0, πBoN is a residual EBM on πθ whose energy is the log win rate of y against samples of πθ. Chow et al. [31] use the variational approximation πBoN(y | x) = πθ(y | x) exp (βN wθ(x, y)) Zθ(x) , wθ(x, y) = Ey′∼πθ(·|x) [1 {r(x, y) ⩾r(x, y′)}] , (167) with βN increasing in N. Since both πθ and the win rate wθ depend on θ, the unnormalized log-density fθ = log πθ + βNwθ has the gradient ∇θfθ(x, y) = ∇θ log πθ(y | x) −βN Ey′∼πθ(·|x) [∇θ log πθ(y′ | x) 1 {r(x, y) < r(x, y′)}] , (168) where the second term differentiates the win rate through the samples of πθ. The two losses below are written in terms of this gradient. Supervised Fine-Tuning. Given expert responses (x, y) ∼D, inference-aware supervised fine-tuning maximizes their likelihood under πBoN rather than under πθ, max θ E(x,y)∼D [log πBoN(y | x)] = E(x,y)∼D [log πθ(y | x) + βN wθ(x, y) −log Zθ(x)] , (169) where Zθ(x) = Ey∼πθ(·|x) [exp (βNwθ(x, y))]. Its gradient is that of maximum likelihood for an EBM Equation 40, E(x,y)∼D [∇θfθ(x, y)] −Ex∼D, y∼πBoN(·|x) [∇θfθ(x, y)] , (170) in which the expert responses are the positives and the responses selected by best-of-N are the negatives. The first term increases the likelihood of the expert responses and their win rate against πθ, and the second lowers the likelihood of the responses that best-of-N already selects, which avoids over-fitting. Reinforcement Learning. With an environment reward R(x, y), which may differ from the verifier score r, inference-aware RL maximizes the reward of the selected response, max θ J(θ) = Ex∼D, y∼πBoN(·|x) [R(x, y)] , ∇θJ(θ) = Ex∼D, y∼πBoN [∇θfθ(x, y) (R(x, y) −b(x))] , (171) with a baseline b(x) = Ey∼πBoN(·|x) [R(x, y)]. This is REINFORCE Equation 32 with the samples drawn from best-of-N instead of from πθ, and since the reward is R rather than r, it also tolerates errors of the verifier. Amortization (Section 7.4) trains πθ to approximate the target on its own, whereas best-of-N samplingaware fine-tuning keeps best-of-N at inference time and trains πθ for it. Writing πBoN as a residual EBM on πθ Equation 167 gives the selection a differentiable density, so supervised fine-tuning becomes maximum likelihood for this EBM, with best-of-N samples as negatives, and RL becomes REINFORCE on best-of-N samples. In both cases the generator is trained as a proposal for best-of-N rather than as a sampler on its own, and it learns to interleave its best responses with more diverse ones, trading exploitation for exploration as N grows. Discussion Throughout this tutorial, we have used EBMs as a single lens on machine learning. This organization grew out of the course CSE 6243 at Georgia Tech, where students appreciated learning machine learning along a

single thread, in which each new method is introduced as a different choice within the same EBM framework, rather than as a catalog of separate model families, tasks, and algorithms, as in the traditional organization of machine learning courses. Any EBM is specified by three choices: the energy, which determines what the model can represent; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We close by summarizing how this view serves three purposes: understanding existing methods, organizing them into one framework, and developing new algorithms. Understanding Existing Literature. Many methods that were developed separately, often under different names and motivations, turn out to be EBMs with particular choices of the three components. In discriminative learning, logistic regression, CRFs, and structured prediction energy networks are conditional EBMs that differ in the structure of the energy over outputs (Section 3). In generative modeling, GANs pair a potential with a learned sampler, normalizing flows and autoregressive models restrict the energy so that the partition function becomes tractable and sampling takes a single pass, diffusion and flow models learn the score of noise-perturbed EBMs, and energy-inspired and deep equilibrium models turn an inference procedure into the model itself (Section 4). In representation learning, contrastive methods including MoCo, word2vec, BERT, diffusion representations, and denoising auto-encoders all learn a bilinear EBM whose factors are the representation, and they differ mainly in the learning method; for the denoising auto-encoder, the bilinear form follows from score matching of a latent-variable EBM (Section 5). Instruction-following retrievers use the same bilinear EBM as a decisive model, by embedding the question as well as the data (Section 5.5). In decision making, maximum-entropy RL, mirror-descent policy updates, and KL-regularized fine-tuning of language models from human feedback yield EBM policies in closed form, and inverse RL and imitation learning fit EBMs from demonstrations (Section 6). Beyond the policy, an EBM world model of the dynamics gives a representation in which value functions are linear (Section 6.4), and planning is inference in an EBM over trajectories (Section 6.5). Inference-time computation in large models, such as best-of-N selection, search over partial solutions, and iterative refinement, consists of samplers for one residual EBM that composes a pretrained generator with a verifier (Section 7). Seen this way, the differences among these methods are differences in how they handle the partition function and sampling, rather than differences in what they model. Organizing the Framework. The three components also organize the methods into a common structure. On the learning side, maximum likelihood, contrastive divergence, NCE, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training share the same gradient and differ only in the sampler that produces the negative samples (Section

a verifier (Section 7). Seen this way, the differences among these methods are differences in how they handle the partition function and sampling, rather than differences in what they model. Organizing the Framework. The three components also organize the methods into a common structure. On the learning side, maximum likelihood, contrastive divergence, NCE, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training share the same gradient and differ only in the sampler that produces the negative samples (Section 2.6). The same axis reappears in every application: SimCLR and CLIP use ranking NCE, SigLIP and word2vec use binary NCE, AmorLIP uses maximum likelihood with an amortized partition function, MoCo uses a fixed-point iteration, and diffusion representations and denoising auto-encoders use score matching (Section 5); maximum-entropy IRL, implicit behavioral cloning, and GAIL fit EBMs from demonstrations by maximum likelihood, NCE, and adversarial training (Section 6.3). On the inference side, MCMC, variational inference, and amortized samplers appear in the same roles, whether the samples are images, tokens, or actions (Section 2.4, Section 6.2, Section 7), and fine-tuning and inference-time computation target the same KL-regularized EBM, differing only in whether its cost is paid during training or at inference (Section 7.4), and best-of-N sampling fine-tuning lies between the two, training the generator for the sampler that uses it (Section 7.5). Placing a method on these axes makes its trade-offs explicit, such as the dependence of NCE on the batch size, the bias of short MCMC chains, or the loss of the global energy in autoregressive reparameterizations, and shows which alternatives are available for each component. Table 3 in Appendix A places every method of this tutorial on these components. Developing New Algorithms. Finally, the framework suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others. Replacing the learning method of a known EBM gives new estimators: fitting the bilinear representation EBM by score matching instead of NCE gives diffusion spectral representations, and by maximum likelihood with an amortized partition function gives AmorLIP (Section 5). Replacing the policy class in RL by an EBM, and its learning by reweighted score matching, gives diffusion policy opti-

mization (Section 6.2). Using the structure of the EBM itself gives new objectives: the smoothed Bellman equation of SBEED, and the value-incentivized regularizers of VAC and VPO, which use the log-partition function of the EBM policy for optimism and pessimism (Section 6.1). Placing the energy on the dynamics gives EBM world models, whose representation makes value functions linear and learnable by temporaldifference learning (Section 6.4). Treating the best-of-N policy itself as a residual EBM gives objectives for distilling it and for fine-tuning the generator for it (Section 7.4, Section 7.5). Using the learned energy itself rather than the representation, with an embedding head for the query and the instruction, gives decisive models that answer new questions in a single forward pass (Section 5.5). Composition is perhaps the most distinctive capability: since the energies of independently trained models can be added to form products of distributions (Section 2.3), as already exploited by classifier and classifier-free guidance (Section 4.3), EBMs provide a principled way to combine pretrained models, constraints, and verifiers at inference time without retraining. In planning, learned dynamics, behavior priors, goals, and constraints each contribute an energy term, and a new task is a new sum of terms (Section 6.5); in reasoning, energies learned for individual constraints are composed to solve problems larger than those seen in training (Section 7.3). We expect this view to remain useful as new models are developed: whenever a model defines an unnormalized score over its outputs, the tools for inference and learning surveyed here apply to it directly. Limitations. The EBM view explains how methods relate, but it does not by itself tell which one works better. Two methods that fit the same energy can behave very differently in practice, since their performance also depends on how the energy is parameterized, on inductive biases such as the architecture and, in contrastive learning, the data augmentations that define the positive pairs, and on the statistical and computational properties of the estimator. The intended use also matters. Methods with the same optimum may serve different purposes, as the denoising auto-encoder and a diffusion model fit the same score at a given noise level but are used for representation and for sampling, respectively; and different uses favor different learning methods: maximum likelihood when calibrated likelihoods are needed, as for density evaluation, score matching when the model is used for sampling, since it learns the score that the sampler follows, and NCE when only relative scores between candidates matter, as in retrieval and ranking. Composition has limitations of its own: the composed distribution is meaningful only when the component energies have compatible scales and the product is normalizable, and sampling from or optimizing the composed landscape can be

when calibrated likelihoods are needed, as for density evaluation, score matching when the model is used for sampling, since it learns the score that the sampler follows, and NCE when only relative scores between candidates matter, as in retrieval and ranking. Composition has limitations of its own: the composed distribution is meaningful only when the component energies have compatible scales and the product is normalizable, and sampling from or optimizing the composed landscape can be much harder than for each component. We therefore suggest that readers weigh these factors together for their own setting, and choose the parameterization of the energy and the methods for learning and inference to the characteristics of the problem. Power-Gas Infrastructure Planning under Weather-induced Supply and Demand Uncertainties Rahman Khorramfar1∗, Dharik Mallapragada2, Saurabh Amin3 1 MIT Energy Initiative (MITEI) and Laboratory for Information & Decision Systems (LIDS), MIT 2 Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering Department, Tandon School of Engineering, New York University 3 Civil and Environmental Engineering (CEE) and LIDS, MIT Abstract Implementing economy-wide decarbonization strategies based on decarbonizing the power grid via variable renewable energy (VRE) expansion and electrification of end-uses requires new approaches for energy infrastructure planning that consider, among other factors, weather-induced uncertainty in demand and VRE supply. An energy planning model that fails to account for these uncertainties can hinder the intended transition efforts to a low-carbon grid and increase the risk of supply shortage especially during extreme weather conditions. Here, we consider the generation and transmission expansion problem of joint power-gas infrastructure and operations planning under the uncertainty of both demand and renewable supply. We propose two distributionally robust optimization approaches based on moment (MDRO) and Wasserstein distance (WDRO) ambiguity sets to endogenize these uncertainties and account for the change in the underlying distribution of these parameters that is caused by the climate change, among other factors. Furthermore, our model considers the risk-aversion of the energy planners in the modeling framework via the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) metric. An equivalent mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) reformulation of both modeling frameworks is presented, and a computationally efficient approximation scheme to obtain near-optimal solutions is proposed. We demonstrate the resulting DRO planning models and solution strategy via a New England case study under different levels of end-use electrification and decarbonization targets. Our experiments systematically explore different modeling aspects and compare the DRO models with stochastic programming (SP) results. Keywords— OR in Energy, Distributionally robust optimization, Generation and transmission expansion, Power and gas infrastructure planning Introduction Power and gas systems are two major energy vectors in modern societies and their long-term planning is the main enabler of the energy transition– a global shift away from the current fossil fuel-based generation to a decarbonized one. However, planning for this transformation is becoming increasingly complex due to evolving generation and consumption patterns, along with factors related to climate change mitigation and adaptation. On one hand, variable renewable energy (VRE) is expected to largely replace fossil-based energy generation. While essential for decarbonization, their inherent intermittent nature poses significant challenges to the planning and operations of energy systems (Moreira et al., 2021). The uncertainty in VRE generation arises not only from short-term weather variability but also from long-term shifts caused by climate change (Staffell and Pfenninger, 2018). On the other hand, the increasing electrification of end-uses, along with the growing deployment of alternative energy carriers ∗Corresponding author: khorram@mit.edu arXiv:2506.23509v3 [eess.SY] 10 Sep 2025

such as biofuel and hydrogen, is fundamentally reshaping the nature of the coupling between gas and electricity infrastructure as the two main energy systems (Von Wald et al., 2022). Consequently, effective planning must account for these uncertainty sources and accurately represent the interdependency between different energy systems. Capacity expansion models are widely used to assess infrastructure needs in response to evolving technologies, demand projections, weather variability, and policy scenarios. Among these, the generation and transmission expansion problem (GTEP) is a well-established framework that provides decision support for long-term energy infrastructure and operations decisions. Defined from a central decisionmaker’s perspective, GTEP integrates the generation expansion problem (GEP) and the transmission expansion problem (TEP). In essence, it determines the optimal sizing, location, generation types, and transmission lines under a set of constraints (Koltsaklis and Dagoumas, 2018). Most GTEPs in the literature adopt models with deterministic parameters and primarily focus on power systems planning, with only a few considering multi-vector infrastructure planning under uncertainty (Klatzer et al., 2022). Despite their widespread use, deterministic models can underor overestimate the required infrastructure, potentially leading to planning outcomes that are vulnerable to extreme weather outcomes. Here, we consider a joint electric power and gas system, focusing on weather-induced uncertainty and its propagation on the uncertain parameters of supply (i.e., capacity factors for VREs) and demand. We develop two distributionally robust optimization (DRO) models to capture these uncertainties and ensure the robustness of the planning outcome toward various weather realizations and distributional shifts due to climate change. GTEP is usually carried out by different entities such as utility companies and system operators. Therefore, our proposed model includes a risk measure to account for the sensitivity of the decision-maker toward extreme parameter values. Developing approaches to capture parameter uncertainties has been the focus of mathematical programming from its early days (Dantzig, 1955). These efforts have led to the emergence of several approaches, among which stochastic programming (SP), robust optimization (RO) and DRO are most notable. SP assumes a perfect characterization of the underlying distribution of uncertainty parameters, usually in the form of discrete scenario realizations. Therefore, the objective of SPs is often time formulated as the expected value of a function that depend on possible realizations. Many studies consider two-stage SP in the context of energy planning. Munoz et al. (2016) propose a two-stage stochastic GTEP under uncertainty of demand and supply potentials of solar, wind and hydropower. Zhan et al. (2016) develop a multistage decision-dependent SP for GEP in which the demand is uncertain and the investment decisions affect the electricity prices. context of energy planning. Munoz et al. (2016) propose a two-stage stochastic GTEP under uncertainty of demand and supply potentials of solar, wind and hydropower. Zhan et al. (2016) develop a multistage decision-dependent SP for GEP in which the demand is uncertain and the investment decisions affect the electricity prices. Coordinated planning of power and gas systems is the focus of some studies that model uncertainty by SP. A GTEP is proposed in (Zhao et al., 2017) under power-gas demand growth uncertainty. A similar approach is proposed in (Nunes et al., 2018) with long-term price and demand growth uncertainties and short-term generation potential of VREs. Despite having mathematical properties that contribute to its performance, the SP has shortcomings that are particularly salient in the context of energy systems planning. First, a proper representation of a distribution may require a large scenario size, leading to the curse of dimensionality and limited tractability of the problem (Moret et al., 2020). Second, it assumes a perfect knowledge of the underlying distribution whereas scenarios are usually based on limited historical records whose distribution can change, for example, due to climate change and energy regulations. Third, SP with discrete scenarios may lead to solutions that perform poorly on out-ofsample scenarios (Bertsimas et al., 2023). In power-gas systems, this may amount to a lack of resiliency and robustness toward extreme scenarios, leading to severe resource inadequacy. Robust optimization partially alleviates SP’s shortcomings by hedging the solution against the worst parameter realization within a specified uncertainty set. RO can be utilized without strong assumptions about the underlying distribution from which uncertain parameters are drawn. A three-stage RO is proposed in (Moreira et al., 2021) for a power system GTEP with renewable and climate uncertainties. In (He et al., 2017), robust optimization is applied to a power-gas GTEP with wind power uncertainty. Two frequent critiques of RO are its over-conservatism and computational burden (Roald et al., 2023). While decision outcomes based on the RO approach can prepare the energy infrastructure for the worst possibilities, it may result in over-investment in certain assets, thus yielding significantly higher system costs. A unifying approach between SP and RO is DRO which offers a way to reduce the conservatism of RO while retaining the tractability of SP (Bertsimas et al., 2023). Since the true distribution of uncertain parameters can be unknown, DRO uses scenarios of random parameters and domain knowledge to limit the true distribution to a family of distributions determined by an ambiguity set. Depending on data availability and application area, the ambiguity sets can be defined considering various fac-

tors including shared moment or discrepancy between distributions (Rahimian and Mehrotra, 2022). Discrepancy-based or metric-based ambiguity sets contain distributions whose probabilistic distance from the nominal empirical distribution is confined to a given positive value. Moment-based approaches build an ambiguity set containing distributions that share a set of moments (e.g., mean, covariance) that satisfy certain properties. While both approaches offer a flexible framework to model uncertainty using partial information, DRO problems with moment-based ambiguity sets are more popular due to computational advantage, interpretability (intuitive statistical measures), and its connection to risk measures (Pourahmadi and Kazempour, 2021). DRO models with metric-based ambiguity sets such as Wasserstein distance have gained popularity in recent years as they offer finite-sample efficiency and strong theoretical foundations, and can admit tractable reformulations (Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn, 2018). The modeling prowess that DRO offers has made it an appealing choice in recent years for various problems in energy systems, including capacity expansion problems (Table 1), distribution system (Zare et al., 2018), smart city energy system design (Li et al., 2023), virtual power plant operations (Cao et al., 2025), critical energy infrastructure (Bellè et al., 2023), and multi-energy systems (Son and Kim, 2024). Planning under uncertainty naturally raises the question of quantifying and managing the risk associated with the worst realization of uncertain parameters. Here, we consider a mean-CVaR objective function to reflect the risk aversion of the decision maker in avoiding high-impact and low-probability scenarios. This objective further allows a trade-off between the expected outcomes and the risk measure. CVaR is a convex and coherent risk measure, making it a common risk index choice in a wide range of applications including energy systems optimization (Roald et al., 2023). The mean-CVaR offers a flexible framework for balancing between the expected value function (risk-neutral) and CVaR measure (risk-averse). Despite the importance of modeling the interdependencies between energy vectors, there is no substantial study for the joint GTEP of power-gas systems, as evident from Table 1. Moreover, most studies consider uncertainty in either supply or demand parameters. This paper bridges the gap in the literature by offering both methodological and practical contributions. First, we present GTEP with CVaR measure for co-optimized power-gas planning as two distributionally robust optimization models to jointly model the uncertainty in demand and supply. The first model is constructed based on a moment-based ambiguity set (MDRO) and the second model based on Wasserstein distance (WDRO). Second, in the MDRO, the proposed ambiguity set embeds spatial correlation between nodes without introducing new set of variables and constraints. Problem Setting We consider general joint power-gas planning problem in which the operations of these two energy systems are interdependent. The planning is carried out for a future target year by which year the system has to satisfy the growing demand and satisfy decarbonization targets among other constraints. In our formulation, power system operates on hourly and gas on daily resolution, both represented by their corresponding network. Following the literature (Teichgraeber and Brandt, 2019), the planner solves the model over a set of representative days. These days are selected and weighted in a way to resemble the operations of the system over the whole planning horizon. In our model, the operations between power and gas systems are interdependent because: i) gas-fired power plants in each power node draw gas from its adjacent gas nodes; ii) the decarbonization target necessitates limiting emissions of CO2 across both systems. Here, the term gas is used to refer to natural gas (NG) and any drop-in low-carbon fuel (low-carbon fuel) such as renewable natural gas that can be transferred through the gas pipelines and have the functionality as NG (Cole et al., 2021). We also assume that demand and supply parameters are given in a time series format. For example, the capacity factor for solar is given per each power node, each planning hour, and each scenario. Let xe and xg be all investment decisions in power and gas systems that are made before the planning horizon (time-independent variables), respectively. For the power system, these variables can include establishing new plants, storage technologies and transmission lines, and/or decommissioning of existing plants. For gas system, xg can represent establishing or decommissioning pipelines. The operational variables of power and gas systems are denoted by ye and yg, respectively. These variables for the power system represent generation, state of storage, flow, load shedding, and CO2 emissions. For the gas system, yg can include decisions such as flow, load shedding, gas import, and CO2 emissions. Also let V denote the set of VRE types (e.g., solar, onshore wind, offshore wind). The assumption here is that the operational problem is feasible for any investment decisions. This is not a restrictive assumption as load-shedding variables can handle any unsatisfied demand. The first term includes i) investment cost for new plants, storage technologies, and transmission lines; ii) fixed operating and maintenance (FOM) cost for plants, storage facilities, and transmission lines; and iii) decommissioning cost for the existing power plants. The second term represents the power system’s operational expenditures including i) variable operating and maintenance (VOM) cost; ii) start-up cost; iii) fuel cost for thermal plants operating on non-gas fuels; and iv) load shedding cost. The third term captures i) investment cost for new pipelines and storage facilities; ii) FOM cost for pipelines and storage facilities; and iii) decommissioning cost of existing pipelines. Finally, the fourth term includes operating expenditures in the gas system including fuel import and load shedding costs. The first set of constraints (1b) represents all constraints in the power system that involve a power load de. Examples include power balance and renewable portfolio standard constraints. Constraints (1c) encapsulate all constraints that involve capacity factors F ν for the renewable generation type ν ∈V. These constraints limits the generation from VRE to their production potential determined by the number of generators and their capacity factors. Similar to power system, constraints (1d) represent all constraints that involve gas demand dg. Finally, constraints (1e) captures all the remaining constraints including i) operating plants determined by existing, new and decommissioned plants, unit commitment, ramping, generation limit for thermal plants, network, storage, and resource availability constraints for power system; ii) operating pipelines, flow, fuel import, and storage for gas system; iii) coupling constraints between power and gas system including the flow of fuel to power system, and joint emissions limit constraints. The constraints (1f) determines the type of variables. Per common models in the literature (Khorramfar et al., 2025), some investment variables are assumed to be integer and the rest of the variables are continuous. The integer variables can represent the number of thermal plants established/decommissioned, and the establishment of transmission lines and pipelines (binary).

However, this can diminish the scalability of the problem (Shehadeh, 2022) and undermine their applicability. Furthermore, the impact of incorporating second-order information on the solution outcome can often be minimal (Basciftci et al., 2023). Some studies seek a remedy, for example by assuming spatially uncorrelated uncertain parameters or solely relying on functions of the first-order information (Hajebrahimi et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022). Instead, we define the ambiguity set that incorporates first-order moment as well as the spatial correlation between energy nodes of the same vector (i.e., power or gas). However, energy planning problems need an efficient solution method that allows a range of sensitivity analyses in a reasonable timeframe. Here, we develop an approximation approach to compute near-optimal solutions of the MILP. This approximation method relied on sequentially solving a series of linear programs to construct a feasible solution, thus the sequential construction method (SCM). The SCM is based on the observation that relaxing certain constraints and variables can significantly increase traceability while retaining key modeling features. Specifically for the problem considered here, relaxing the network constraints, relaxing the integrality of integer variables, and/or setting the integer variables to given values yields a model with significantly less computational burden. Case Study and Computational Setup We formulate the DRO model for the joint planning of electricity-gas infrastructure, adapting operational constraints from the previously published deterministic model, JPoNG (Khorramfar et al., 2024). JPoNG determines the cost-optimal planning decisions for power and gas systems under a detailed representation of both systems’ constraints. It allows different planning resolutions for each system; the power system operates on an hourly basis whereas daily resolution is the operational granularity of the gas system. In our adapted formulation, the first stage decisions include establishing new power plants and battery storage, decommissioning existing power plants, establishing new transmission lines and pipelines, and decommissioning existing pipelines. The operational variables for the electric power system include power generation, storage, power flow, load shedding, and emissions amount. The gas network’s operational variables consist of gas flow, NG and low-carbon fuel import, load shedding, and emissions amount. Our formulation represents the main investment and operational constraints. For the power systems, it includes operational plants, power balance, generation limit, ramping, load shedding limit, direct current approximation of the network flow, storage limit, storage state-of-charge, and land-use availability for VRE (resource availability). For the gas system, the constraints include operational pipelines, demand and supply balance, linearized network flow, gas and low-carbon fuel import limit, and storage constraints. The operations of both systems are interconnected through two sets of constraints. The first coupling constraints ensure the flow of gas to gas-fired plants in the power system, and the second set limits the CO2 emission incurred by consuming NG in both systems. Discrete decision variables in the model include number of thermal and nuclear plants installed (integer) and candidate pipeline and transmission line added (binary variables). The rest of the variables are continuous. The objective function of the formulated DRO model is to minimize the investment and operational costs for both power and gas systems. The investment cost includes i) investment cost in new generation technologies, ii) network expansion (transmission lines and pipelines), iii) decommissioning cost for the existing power plants and pipeline, and iv) storage cost. The operational costs include i) variable operating and maintenance costs (VOM) for power plants, ii) fixed operating and maintenance cost (FOM) for power plants,

We consider the case study of New England to explore electricity and gas infrastructure investments and operations under future scenarios with stringent CO2 emissions constraints and varying degrees of end-use electrification in the building sector. The New England region’s spatial representation in the model, shown in Fig. 2a, consists of: a) a power network with 6 nodes (one node per state) connected by 23 exiting transmission lines and 40 candidate lines, b) a gas network with 23 nodes connected by 28 existing and 36 candidate pipelines. The power system has 8 generation types, of which 3 are existing generation types and the rest are new ones. Existing power plant types include ‘ng’ (gas-fired plants), ‘hydro’, and ‘nuclear’. The new plant types are ‘CCGT’ (combined cycle gas turbine), ‘CCGT-CCS’ (CCGT with carbon capture and storage technology that can capture 90% of the resulting emissions), ‘solar-new’, ‘wind-new’, and ‘wind-offshore’. The storage system is assumed to be the short-duration Lithium-ion grid-scale batteries. The gas infrastructure is served by supplying gas from two sources: a) NG with cost of 5.45$/MMBtu depending on supply source and b) low-carbon fuel, representing synthetic or biomass-derived methane, that can be used with the existing infrastructure but comes at a substantial cost premium (20 $/MMBtu vs. 5.45 $/MMBtu for NG). The low-carbon fuel is assumed to have zero CO2 emissions owing to the biogenic nature of the CO2 source. The full description of the model is given in Appendix E. The model outcomes are evaluated for 3 end-use electrification levels and two different decarbonization levels (detailed in Khorramfar et al. (2025)). The end-use electrification levels represent a different degree of electrification for the residential building sector in the New England region of the US, with the lowest electrification corresponding to the reference case (RF), followed by medium (ME) and high

(HE) electrification levels. We also consider 80% and 95% decarbonization targets as all New England states have an emissions reduction goal of 80% by 2050 below the baseline year of 1990 with some having a goal as high as 95%. The reference (Khorramfar et al., 2025) provides 20 projections of supply and demand data for the year 2050 for each of the electrification levels. The authors develop a bottom-up model that outputs a projection based on historical supply and demand data, among others. Therefore, the number of projections is limited by the available historical data for the regions, in this case 20 years. Note that each projection is treated as a realization of uncertainty. For each realization, the supply data consists of the capacity factors for solar, onshore wind, and offshore wind generators, and the demand data includes the bulk electric power and gas demand. The realization of uncertain parameters show significant interannual variation as illustrated in the case of electricity demand in Fig. 2b. We set the value of lost load for power and gas systems at 10,000 $/MWh and $10,000 $/MMBtu, respectively. The value of all other parameters is adopted from (Khorramfar et al., 2024) and (Khorramfar et al., 2025). 6.2 Importance of Uncertainty To show the importance of considering uncertainty in weather-induced parameters, we calculate the Value of Stochastic Programming (VSS) and the Expected value of the Perfect Information (EVPI). Both of these measures are common criteria in the stochastic programming literature each revealing an aspect of using stochastic models over deterministic solutions (Birge and Louveaux, 2011). VSS quantifies the expected gain from solving an SP compared to its deterministic counterpart. VSS is calculated in two steps. In the first step, the problem is solved with all random variables replaced by their statistical means. In the second step, the SP is solved such that the value of the first stage variables are set to their values in the first step (Zhao et al., 2017). In case of little to no uncertainty, the VSS approaches zero, indicating that the deterministic solution is a good approximation for the problem. Future planning models often rely on prediction and projection methods to estimate the possible realization of random parameters. EVPI is a measure to quantify the value of perfect tools to determine the exact realization of scenarios. In other words, EVPI is the upper bound for the price that the planner should be willing to pay in the long run in order to have access to precise outcomes of the uncertain parameters (Birge and Louveaux, 2011). EVPI is calculated by solving the deterministic case for each scenario independently and then aggregating the objective values by their corresponding probabilities. Table 3 shows the normalized values for VSS and EVPI. The solution of VSS is normalized by dividing the difference between the VSS solution and the original SP solution by the SP solution. The EVPI values are normalized in a similar fashion. With values ranging from 178 to 379%, the VSS shows that the use of stochastic programming is highly recommended, especially under higher electrification levels. It is worth noting that the VSS values largely depend on the value of load shedding for the power system. This is because once the first stage variables are fixed, the system results in a solution with substantial load shedding, hence the higher the load shedding cost, the higher the VSS. As such, reducing or increasing the load-shedding cost for power and gas systems can significantly impact the values. However, the amount of load shedding indicates that the deterministic model can lead to a system that is severely unreliable for some weather outcomes. The EVPI values indicate the share of the SP objective values that the planners should be willing to pay for perfect information. Conclusion In this paper, we considered a joint planning of electric power and gas systems as a GTEP, and proposed a framework to characterize power and gas demand as well as the supply of renewable generation via distributionally robust optimization. Our modeling approach incorporated the risk sensitivity of the energy planner as conditional value-at-risk to hedge against the worst realization of parameters. We developed DRO models with both moment and metric-based (Wasserstein distance) ambiguity sets.

In the moment-based model, we enriched the ambiguity set by the correlation between power-gas nodes, and showed that both models can be formulated as MILP problems. The resulting MILP is a large-scale model that is intractable to solve in larger sizes. Therefore, we developed an efficient approximation scheme that relies on solving a sequence of linear programs to construct a feasible solution. Our modeling approach is applied to future energy planning of the New England region under different emissions reduction goals as well as levels of residential heating electrification which impacts the long-term projection of power-gas demands. Finally, our extensive numerical analyses highlight the challenges surrounding energy transition as pertained to weather-induced uncertainty and shed light on various aspects of the modeling approach. First, our analyses show that planning under uncertainty is indispensable to achieving a more reliable future energy system, otherwise the system may face insufficient generation capacity or misplaced assets leading to severe blackout events. Second, disregarding power system’s interdependence with gas can distort outcomes, resulting in lower system cost in less ambitious decarbonization targets and vice versa for more stringent emissions limit. Third, the complementarity effect between capacity factors and demand is substantial, especially under DRO models. Although excluding either demand or supply uncertainty can lead to different outcomes, the results suggest that demand uncertainty is a better proxy for uncertainties posed by the weather. Fourth, the energy transition involves a vast array of stakeholders whose risk sensitivities should be considered as part of the modeling framework. Finally, the experiments highlighted the inherent uncertainty in weather-induced parameters and quantified the out-ofsample performance of each modeling approach. From the modeling perspective, the theme of our study is two-fold. First, we stress the role of the modeling approach in characterizing uncertainty. While there are many paradigms to endogenize uncertainty, energy transition planners should opt for modeling tools that better describe the type of uncertainty and available data. Second, the scalability of energy planning models is a persistent challenge despite advances in recent years. Although the exact solution methods provide optimality guarantees, their timeframe can be prohibitively long to conduct a range of sensitivity analyses which is an important aspect in energy planning models. Future directions are envisioned to investigate other key dimensions of the planning under uncertainty. The DRO models developed for discrete realizations can be extended to handle continuous ambiguity sets that cover an ensemble of projections. The resulting model can present nonconvexity, therefore, future works can consider ML-assisted optimization models to not only streamline the solution process but also to generate synthetic projections with varying degrees of extremities. The approximate solution method presented here performs efficiently for a limited number of representative days, but it may fail

planning under uncertainty. The DRO models developed for discrete realizations can be extended to handle continuous ambiguity sets that cover an ensemble of projections. The resulting model can present nonconvexity, therefore, future works can consider ML-assisted optimization models to not only streamline the solution process but also to generate synthetic projections with varying degrees of extremities. The approximate solution method presented here performs efficiently for a limited number of representative days, but it may fail in larger sizes. A decomposition method that can utilize the problem structure can be developed to further address the problem’s scalability. Beyond the aforementioned directions, future endeavors can augment the modeling fidelity. This study adopts a central planner perspective, whereas in practice there are multiple entities such as government agencies, utility companies and balancing authorities that are involved in energy infrastructure planning. Therefore, a decentralized approach that captures the main interdependence between these entities can offer a higher fidelity model. Eventually, future studies can encompass uncertainties in other parameters as future energy planning is subject to myriads of unpredictabilities stemming from fluctuating prices, climate change trends, investment costs, regulations, and geopolitical factors among others. X k∈Aen fge knτ = X t∈Teτ X i∈G hipntis n ∈N e, τ ∈R (32a) Ee s = X n∈N e X t∈T e X i∈G wts(1 −ηi)ηghipntis Eg s = X k∈N g X τ∈T g ηg(Dg kτs −aLCF kτ −ag kτs) Ee s + Eg s ≤(1 −ζ)(Ue emis + Ug emis) (32b)

The first coupling constraints (32a) capture the flow of gas to the power network for each node and at each time period. The variable Ee s accounts for CO2 emission due to the consumption of gas in the power system. The variable Eg s computes the emission from the gas system by subtracting the demand from LCF consumption and gas load shedding. The second coupling constraint (32b) ensures that the net CO2 emissions associated with the power-gas system are below a pre-specified threshold value, which is defined based on a baseline (e.g., historical) emissions level. The first term is the emissions due to non-power gas consumption (i.e., gas consumption in the gas system such as space heating, industry use, and transportation). Since the model does not track whether LCF is used to meet non-power gas demand or for power generation, the first term computes gross emissions from all gas use presuming it is all fossil and then subtracts emissions benefits from using LCF. F Sequential Construction Method for the Stochastic Program This section details the Sequential Construction Method (SCM) for the model presented in section (E). 1. Solve MILPref with the following simplifications and get the solution ¯X: • Remove all network constraints for the power system and get the copper-plate model. In effect, the constrains (2g) and (2h) are removed from the model presented in section (E), and the constraint (2f) becomes the following for all t ∈T e X n∈N e  X i∈P pntis + X r∈Sen (seDis ntr −seCh ntrs) + ae nts  = X n∈N e De nϕe ts • Relax the integrality of integer variables xop ni, xest ni , xdec ni , zelnv ℓ , zglnv ℓ , zgDec ℓ , zgOp ℓ 2. Solve MILPref with the following simplifications and constraints and get the solution ˆX: • Relax the integrality of integer variables xop ni, xest ni , xdec ni , zelnv ℓ , zglnv ℓ , zgDec ℓ , zgOp ℓ • For thermal plants, set xop ni = ⌊(¯xop ni)⌉, n ∈N, i ∈H, where ⌊x⌉is the rounding operator that returns the nearest integer value to x, and ¯xop ni is the value of the variable in previous step • For VRE plants, add constraints xop ni = ⌊¯xop ni⌋, n ∈N, i ∈V, where ⌊x⌋is the floor operator that returns the greatest integer less than or equal to x, and ¯xop ni is the value of the variable in previous step. • Add constraints zgOp ℓ = 1 if ¯zgOp ℓ ≥ϵ1, and zgOp ℓ = 0, otherwise. ¯zgOp ℓ is the value of the variable in previous step 3. Solve MILPref with the following simplifications and constraints

constraints xop ni = ⌊¯xop ni⌋, n ∈N, i ∈V, where ⌊x⌋is the floor operator that returns the greatest integer less than or equal to x, and ¯xop ni is the value of the variable in previous step. • Add constraints zgOp ℓ = 1 if ¯zgOp ℓ ≥ϵ1, and zgOp ℓ = 0, otherwise. ¯zgOp ℓ is the value of the variable in previous step 3. Solve MILPref with the following simplifications and constraints and get feasible solution X∗: • Set xop ni = ˆxop ni, n ∈N, i ∈H, where ˆxop ni is the value of the variable in previous step. • Set zgOp ℓ = ˆzgOp ℓ , where ˆzgOp ℓ is the value of the variable in previous step. • Add constraints zeInv ℓ = 1 if ˆzeInv ℓ > ϵ2, and zeInv ℓ = 0, otherwise. ˆzeInv ℓ is the value of the variable in previous step. In our experiments, ϵ1 = 0.01 and ϵ2 = 0.3.
